_about: Sayings, idioms, slang and cultural references for sayings.py, written by Muse Spark (tools/make_sayings.py) and checked by a second pass. lexicon.json stays the hand-made list.

forms: తింటే గారెలు తినాలి, వింటే భారతం వినాలి
te.roman: tinte gaarelu tinaali, vinte bhaaratam vinaali
te.literal: if eat, must eat gaarelu; if listen, must listen Bharatam
te.translate_as: If you do something, do the best of it.
te.note: Grandmothers say it teasingly when serving special snacks or urging to choose the best.

te.literal: hunger knows not taste, sleep knows not comfort
te.translate_as: A hungry person eats anything; a sleepy person sleeps anywhere.
te.note: Said when children complain about taste or want special food.

te.literal: to house that gave rice, do not dig a hole
te.translate_as: Do not betray or harm one who fed and helped you.
te.note: Said to teach gratitude toward those who give food and shelter.

te.translate_as: Result matches the effort and material used.
te.note: Said in the kitchen when explaining why quantity or quality turned out as it did.

te.literal: he will not shoo even a crow with dirty eating hand
te.translate_as: He is extremely stingy, will not share food.
te.note: Grandmothers use it to scold a miser who will not offer even leftovers.

te.literal: like counting rafters of the house where you ate
te.translate_as: Being ungrateful and finding fault after enjoying hospitality.
te.note: Said when someone criticizes the food or family after being fed.

te.literal: if you eat salt, you must drink water
te.translate_as: One who does wrong must face punishment/consequence.
te.note: Often said while cooking or eating to teach responsibility for actions.

te.literal: like thrown away like curry leaf in curry
te.translate_as: Used for flavor then discarded when no longer needed.
te.note: Elders say it when someone feels used and ignored after helping.

te.literal: mother-in-law will not serve, nor let beg and eat
te.translate_as: Obstructive person neither helps nor lets others help.
te.note: Grandmothers say it about strict in-laws and food control in joint families.

forms: ఆవు చేలో మేస్తే దూడ గట్టున మేస్తుందా
te.roman: aavu chenu meste, doodaa gattuna mestundaa
te.literal: if cow grazes the crop, will calf graze on the bund
te.translate_as: Children copy elders; if elders misbehave, children will too.
te.note: Said at meals to remind parents to set a good eating example.

te.literal: when soft food was served, he said teeth fell out
te.translate_as: Finding excuses despite getting easy, good food.
te.note: Said when children make excuses instead of eating soft tasty food.

forms: అడిగేవాడికి చెప్పేవాడు లోకువ, తినేవాడికి వడ్డించేవాడు లోకువ
te.roman: adigevaadiki cheppevaadu lokuva, tinevaadiki vaddinchevaadu lokuva
te.literal: to asker teller is cheap, to eater server is cheap
te.translate_as: People undervalue one who gives food or advice freely.
te.note: Elders say it when guests demand more without thanking the cook.

te.literal: while about to eat, why tastes
te.translate_as: Do not demand perfect taste when food is ready to eat.
te.note: Grandmothers say it to stop picky talk at serving time.

te.literal: like drinking milk and kicking the breast
te.translate_as: Harming the very one who nourished you.
te.note: Said to warn against ingratitude toward mother or provider of food.

forms: అన్నమో రామచంద్రా అంటే ఆకులో పిండివంట కావాలన్నాడట
te.roman: annamo raamachandraa ante aakulo pindivanta annaadata
te.literal: when he said food oh Ramachandra, he said leaf has pindivanta
te.translate_as: A beggar in need still demands a feast.
te.note: Said laughingly when someone is hungry but still picky about the menu.

forms: అత్త మీది కోపం దుత్త మీద చూపినట్టు
te.roman: atta meedi kopam dutta meeda choopinattu
te.literal: like showing anger at mother-in-law on the water-pot
te.translate_as: Taking out anger on someone else instead of the real person.
te.note: Grandmothers say it when there is tension between aththa and kodalu in the house.

forms: అత్త లేని కోడలు ఉత్తమురాలు, కోడలు లేని అత్త గుణవంతురాలు
te.roman: atta leni kodalu uttamuraalu, kodalu leni atta gunavanturaalu
te.literal: a daughter-in-law without mother-in-law is best, a mother-in-law without daughter-in-law is virtuous
te.translate_as: In-law fights are seen as natural and unavoidable.
te.note: Said with a smile when aththa-kodalu argue, to mean both sides look good only when apart.

forms: తల్లిని మించిన దైవము లేదు, గాయత్రిని మించిన మంత్రము లేదు
te.roman: tallini minchina daivam ledu, gayatrini minchina mantram ledu
te.literal: there is no god greater than mother, no mantra greater than Gayatri
te.translate_as: Mother is the highest god, and Gayatri is the highest mantra.
te.note: Elders say it to teach children to respect and serve their mother first.

te.literal: see the mother and marry the daughter
te.translate_as: A girl’s nature is judged by her mother and family.
te.note: Said at marriage talks when checking the bride’s family background.

te.literal: the wife is the lamp of the house
te.translate_as: The woman makes the home bright and orderly.
te.note: Said to praise a wife’s role in keeping family life together.

te.literal: for own people in leaves, for others in metal plates
te.translate_as: people favour outsiders and neglect their own relatives
te.note: Said when relatives complain of partiality at feasts or help.

forms: దూరపు చుట్టం కంటే దగ్గరి పొరుగు మేలు
te.roman: doorapu chuttam kante daggari porugu melu
te.literal: a near neighbour is better than a distant relative
te.translate_as: neighbours help first in need, not far-off kin
te.note: Said to value good neighbours when relatives live far away.

te.literal: even god cannot catch a thief from inside the house
te.translate_as: it is very hard to guard against betrayal by family
te.note: Said when money or secrets are lost because of someone inside the family.

te.translate_as: children or siblings are not all the same
te.note: Said to parents not to compare brothers, sisters or children.

forms: కన్నతల్లి కడుపు చూస్తుంది, కట్టుకున్నది జేబు చూస్తుంది
te.roman: kannatalli kadupu choostundi, kattukunnadi jebu choostundi
te.literal: birth mother looks at stomach, wife looks at pocket
te.translate_as: mother cares if you ate, wife cares about money
te.note: Said half-jokingly about the different love of mother and wife.

forms: అమ్మ పాలు తాగి రమ్మంటే అత్త పాలు తాగి వచ్చినట్టు
te.roman: amma paalu taagi rammante, atta paalu taagi vachchinattu
te.literal: like mother asked to drink her milk and go, he drank mother-in-law’s milk and came
te.translate_as: taking unduly long time to come back, delaying badly
te.note: Said when a child or new family member overdoes what elders asked.

forms: పెళ్లి చేసి చూడు, ఇల్లు కట్టి చూడు
te.roman: pelli chesi choodu, illu katti choodu
te.literal: do a marriage and see, build a house and see
te.translate_as: marriage and house-building are difficult, costly tasks known only by doing them
te.note: Said to young people who think marriage and family life are easy.

te.literal: there is no alliance greater than cousin alliance
te.translate_as: marriage among close relatives keeps families united
te.note: Said during matches when preferring mena-mama or mena-atta children.

forms: తల్లిదండ్రుల మీద దయలేని పుత్రుడు పుట్టనేమి వాడు గిట్టనేమి
te.roman: tallidandrula meeda dayaleni putrudu puttanemi vaadu gittanemi
te.literal: what if a son without kindness to parents is born, what if he dies
te.translate_as: a child who does not care for parents is useless
te.note: A Vemana verse elders quote to stress serving parents in old age.

forms: అప్పు చేసి పప్పు కూడు తినడం కంటే ఉప్పుతో గంజి తాగడం మేలు
te.roman: appu chesi pappu kudu tinadam kante upputo ganji tagadam melu
te.literal: Better to drink gruel with salt peacefully than to eat dal-rice on borrowed money
te.translate_as: Do not live on debt to show off; live within means.
te.note: Grandmothers say it when children want expensive things on credit.

te.literal: Taking a loan is laughter, repaying it is crying
te.translate_as: Borrowing is easy, repaying is hard.
te.note: Said to warn young people before taking loans.

te.literal: This whole world is rooted in money
te.translate_as: Money drives much of the world.
te.note: Elders quote it to explain why money must be respected and earned honestly.

te.literal: Like what happened to Pullayya when he stood surety
te.translate_as: If you guarantee someone's debt, you will suffer.
te.note: Said when someone is asked to sign as guarantor for a loan.

te.literal: The lender becomes a beggar, the borrower becomes a king
te.translate_as: Lenders have to beg for their own money back.
te.note: Said when someone hesitates to lend because repayment is difficult.

forms: కలిమి గలవాడే కులీనుడు, బలిమి గలవాడే బంధువుడు
te.roman: kalimi galavade kulinudu, balimi galavade bandhuvudu
te.literal: Only the rich man is noble, only the strong man is kin
te.translate_as: People respect wealth and power.
te.note: Elders say it sadly to explain how society favours the rich.

te.literal: Curry according to the coin paid
te.translate_as: You get what you pay for.
te.note: Said while bargaining to explain cheap price means cheap quality.

forms: చేతి చమురు వదిలితే గాని పని కాదు
te.roman: cheti chamuru vadilite gani pani kadu
te.literal: Work will not happen unless grease leaves the hand
te.translate_as: Nothing moves without a bribe or spending money.
te.note: Said about corruption when money must be paid to get work done.

te.literal: Riches and poverty are like two pots on a shoulder-pole
te.translate_as: Wealth and poverty keep alternating in life.
te.note: Said to console someone who lost money that bad times will pass.

te.literal: Like selling fruits by naming another’s tree
te.translate_as: Living off another's name or credit without owning anything.
te.note: Said when someone borrows or shows off using family wealth.

te.translate_as: Wasteful spending leads to suffering.
te.note: A common warning against lavish spending and show-off weddings.

te.translate_as: Excessive greed brings disaster.
te.note: Elders say it when someone chases quick money or too much profit.

te.translate_as: Some natures/habits never change.
te.note: Grandparents say it when someone keeps repeating a bad habit despite advice.

te.literal: by cat curses hanging pots will not break
te.translate_as: Jealous curses cannot harm you.
te.note: Said to comfort a child when others are jealous or speak badly.

te.literal: crow baby is dear to crow
te.translate_as: Every parent loves their own child.
te.note: Said lovingly about parents doting on their children.

te.translate_as: A good thing in the hands of one who cannot use it.
te.note: Said when someone gets something valuable but does not know how to handle it.

te.literal: what does donkey know of sandalwood smell
te.translate_as: A fool cannot appreciate fine things.
te.note: Said when someone fails to value good food, music, or advice.

te.literal: like pouring milk for a snake
te.translate_as: Helping a bad person will backfire.
te.note: Elders warn with this when kindness is shown to an ungrateful person.

te.literal: like fox branding itself seeing tiger
te.translate_as: Imitating the powerful beyond one's capacity brings self-harm.
te.note: Said when children imitate dangerous or unsuitable behavior.

te.translate_as: Something big becomes insignificant/has no effect when swallowed by something huge.
te.note: Said when a big effort or loss makes no difference to a rich or big person.

forms: ఆవు చేను మేస్తే దూడ గట్టున మేస్తుందా
te.roman: aavu chelo meste duda gattuna mestundaa
te.literal: if cow grazes in field will calf graze on bund
te.translate_as: Children follow parents' example.
te.note: Said to remind parents that children copy their behavior.

te.literal: like saying bull gave birth so tie the calf
te.translate_as: Believing nonsense without thinking.
te.note: Said when someone believes rumors or impossible stories.

te.translate_as: Fake dignity with no real worth.
te.note: Said teasingly when someone acts proud without reason.

te.translate_as: A fitting reply to a low attack.
te.note: Said to justify giving a strong answer to insults.

te.literal: if rooster does not crow will it not dawn
te.translate_as: The world goes on without you; nothing stops for one person's absence.
te.note: Elders say it when someone thinks they are indispensable.

te.literal: like cat drinking milk with eyes closed
te.translate_as: Thinking no one sees your secret act.
te.note: Said when a child does mischief thinking elders will not notice.

te.translate_as: Small efforts add up to a big result.
te.note: Grandparents say it when saving grain, money, or doing farm work little by little.

te.literal: what does not bend as sapling will it bend as tree
te.translate_as: Habits must be taught young.
te.note: Said about children, using the familiar farm image of a young plant.

te.literal: bull's wound is feast to crow
te.translate_as: Others enjoy our suffering.
te.note: Said when neighbours take advantage of someone's trouble, from village cattle life.

te.literal: when asked who stole pumpkins he touched his shoulders
te.translate_as: A guilty person betrays himself.
te.note: Said when someone reacts guiltily, from stealing pumpkins off a farm.

forms: ఇల్లు కట్టి చూడు పెళ్లి చేసి చూడు
te.roman: illu katti choodu pelli chesi choodu
te.literal: build house and see marry and see
te.translate_as: Only experience teaches how hard big duties are.
te.note: Village elders say it about the cost and trouble of building a house and arranging marriage.

te.literal: rain's coming life's going not known
te.translate_as: Rain and death are unpredictable.
te.note: Farmers say it about depending on rain and the uncertainty of life.

te.translate_as: Excess rain is as bad as drought.
te.note: Said about farming seasons and also about going to extremes in anything.

forms: అడ్డాలనాడు బిడ్డలైనా గాని గడ్డాలనాడు గడ్డి కూడా కాదు
te.roman: addaala naadu biddalainaa gaani gaddaala naadu gaddi koodaa kaadu
te.literal: children in Ashadham okay but grass in Magham not even
te.translate_as: Sowing must be done in the right season.
te.note: Old farming saying about timely sowing in the rainy season to get a crop.

te.literal: water knows lowland truth God knows
te.translate_as: Water flows down, only God knows the truth.
te.note: Said in village disputes, comparing water finding its level to truth coming out.

te.literal: like village joining to dig tank
te.translate_as: Unity makes big work possible.
te.note: Said when villagers work together, recalling community tanks and wells.

te.translate_as: You face the results of your actions.
te.note: Said about good or bad deeds, straight from sowing and harvesting the crop.

te.literal: with hard work, there is no famine
te.translate_as: Hard work prevents poverty.
te.note: Grandparents say it to encourage farming, studying, or steady work.

te.translate_as: Hard work brings reward.
te.note: Said briefly to remind children that results need effort.

te.literal: if you sit and eat, even hills will melt away
te.translate_as: Without earning, even great wealth runs out.
te.note: Said to warn against laziness and wasting savings.

te.literal: do not take hold lightly, once held do not let go
te.translate_as: Be firm and finish what you start.
te.note: Said to teach determination in work and promises.

forms: తవ్విన కొద్దీ ఊట, చదివిన కొద్దీ జ్ఞానం
te.roman: tavvina koddi oota, chadivina koddi gnaanam
te.literal: the more you dig, water; the more you read, knowledge
te.translate_as: Consistent effort gives more results.
te.note: Said especially about studies and steady practice.

te.translate_as: Patience and careful, unhurried work matter most.
te.note: Said when rushing work and making mistakes.

te.literal: unless the baby cries, even the mother will not give milk
te.translate_as: You must ask and try; nothing comes by itself, even a mother will not give milk unless the child cries.
te.note: Said to push shy children to speak up and make effort.

te.literal: like digging a mountain and catching a mouse
te.translate_as: Huge effort for a tiny result.
te.note: Said when hard work is wasted by poor planning.

te.literal: like holding leaves after hands are burnt
te.translate_as: Acting too late is useless, like holding leaves after hands are burnt.
te.note: Said when someone works only after the loss happens.

te.literal: by practice, tasks succeed in this world
te.translate_as: Through means/practice/perseverance any work can be accomplished.
te.note: From Vemana, quoted by elders to stress daily practice.

te.literal: he who achieves what he resolves is a man
te.translate_as: He alone is a real man who achieves what he resolves.
te.note: Said to praise follow-through and challenge laziness.

te.literal: there is no medicine greater than patience
te.translate_as: There is no better remedy/medicine than patience.
te.note: Said during long, tiring work to keep going calmly.

te.literal: a full pot does not slosh
te.translate_as: Truly knowledgeable people stay humble and calm, only the half-knowledgeable boast.
te.note: Grandparents say it when someone brags to remind them real greatness is quiet.

te.translate_as: Excess should be avoided everywhere; too much of anything causes harm.
te.note: Elders quote it to warn against going overboard in pride or show-off.

te.translate_as: Real learning gives humility; education should make you humble, not arrogant.
te.note: Grandparents say it to teach that educated people must bow, not boast.

forms: అల్పుడికి ఐశ్వర్యం వస్తే అర్ధరాత్రి గొడుగు తెమ్మన్నాడట
te.roman: alpuniki aishvaryam vaste ardharaatri godugu temmannadata
te.literal: when a petty man got wealth, he asked for an umbrella at midnight
te.translate_as: When a small-minded/low person gets wealth, he becomes arrogant and showy, as if asking for an umbrella at midnight.
te.note: Grandmothers say it when someone with new status acts bossy.

te.literal: if there is one who kicks the buttock, there is one who kicks his head
te.translate_as: However powerful and proud you are, someone stronger is above you.
te.note: Said to cut down bullies who think no one can touch them.

te.literal: do not do gymnastics leaving the ground
te.translate_as: Do not do fencing/stunts leaving the ground; do not act without a base/support, do not be unrealistic.
te.note: Elders say it when children act too modern or superior.

te.literal: however tall you grow, you must stay bent low
te.translate_as: However much one rises in life, one should remain humble.
te.note: A classic grandmother blessing-warning to successful grandchildren.

te.literal: if you stay low and quiet, everything will come
te.translate_as: If one stays humble and submissive, one will gain everything.
te.note: Said to advise patience and modesty over demanding proudly.

te.translate_as: Excessive pride causes one's downfall.
te.note: Grandparents say it after stories of kings and rich men who fell from pride.

te.literal: like a monkey getting a coconut
te.translate_as: Like a monkey getting a coconut; a fool getting something valuable without knowing how to use it.
te.note: Said when someone mishandles a good opportunity or gift.

te.literal: trying to make a priest, it became a monkey
te.translate_as: Trying to make a priest and making a monkey instead; a bungled attempt to do good ends in a mess.
te.note: Said when well-meant meddling makes things worse.

te.literal: an empty pot makes more sound
te.translate_as: An empty pot makes the most noise; ignorant people talk the loudest.
te.note: Said when someone talks big without real knowledge.

te.literal: like falling into a pit knowingly
te.translate_as: Like falling into a pit knowingly; doing wrong even after knowing it is wrong.
te.note: Said to scold someone who makes a knowing mistake.

te.literal: like a blind man feeling an elephant
te.translate_as: Like blind men feeling an elephant; judging the whole by a touched part.
te.note: Told to explain why people argue foolishly without full knowledge.

te.literal: like a monkey scratching its wound
te.translate_as: Like a monkey scratching its wound; foolishly making a small problem worse.
te.note: Said when someone keeps bringing up a settled quarrel.

te.literal: like firing a Brahmastra at a sparrow
te.translate_as: Like firing the Brahmastra at a sparrow; using massive means for a tiny job.
te.note: Said when someone overreacts to a small matter.

te.translate_as: Over-cleverness brings danger; being too smart for one's own good leads to trouble.
te.note: Elders say it when a child tries to be too clever and gets caught.

te.literal: like putting a ladder to the sky
te.translate_as: Like putting a ladder to the sky; an impossible, foolish plan.
te.note: Said to laugh at unrealistic big talk.

te.literal: bringing an axe for what a fingernail could remove
te.translate_as: Bringing an axe for what a fingernail could remove; making a simple task needlessly complicated.
te.note: Said when someone uses heavy means for an easy job.

te.literal: she who cannot climb to the utti, will she climb to heaven
te.translate_as: Can she who cannot climb the hanging pot-rack climb to heaven; one who fails at little things cannot achieve big things.
te.note: Grandmothers tease with this when children ignore basic work.

te.literal: like a blind ox falling into the field
te.translate_as: Like a blind bull entering a field; blundering in and ruining everything.
te.note: Said when someone enters a matter blindly and spoils it.

te.literal: like the jackal branding itself seeing the tiger
te.translate_as: Like the jackal branding itself after seeing the tiger; foolishly imitating the great beyond one's capacity.
te.note: Said when someone imitates others blindly and harms themselves.

te.literal: a pestle blow on a whitlow
te.translate_as: tit for tat; a strong befitting counterblow
te.note: Said when someone gives a fitting tit-for-tat reply to a schemer.

te.literal: like a cat drinking milk with eyes closed
te.translate_as: thinking no one sees your trick
te.note: Said when someone does something sneaky in the open and thinks others don't notice.

te.literal: like swimming the Godavari holding a dog's tail
te.translate_as: a foolish impossible plan relying on useless support that will fail
te.note: Grandparents say it when someone relies on a useless trick for a big job.

te.translate_as: a cleverer counter-move
te.note: Said admiringly when someone outsmarts a schemer with a bigger trick.

te.literal: like teaching swimming to a baby fish
te.translate_as: trying to teach an expert what they already know
te.note: Said when a novice tries to show cleverness to someone who knows more.

te.literal: grapes are sour for the fox
te.translate_as: pretending you don't want what you can't get
te.note: Said when someone fails by cunning and then dismisses the prize as worthless.

te.literal: even if you feed milk to a snake, it spits only venom
te.translate_as: a wicked nature never changes despite good treatment
te.note: Said to warn not to trust a deceitful person even if treated kindly.

te.literal: the bird is small, its chirp is great
te.translate_as: small in size but great in talent or effect
te.note: Said proudly when a small child speaks very cleverly.

te.literal: like a wood-apple stuck in the throat
te.translate_as: stuck in a dilemma, able neither to swallow nor spit out
te.note: Said when clever scheming traps a person so they can neither admit nor deny.

te.roman: taadini tannevaadunte vaadi tala dannevaadu untaadu
te.literal: if there is one who kicks the palmyra, there is one who kicks his head
te.translate_as: there is always someone stronger or cleverer than the strong or clever
te.note: Grandmothers say it to humble a boastful smart person.

te.literal: like a woman who can't jump to the pot-hanger jumping to heaven
te.translate_as: one unable to do a small task claiming a huge task; ambition beyond capacity
te.note: Said when someone fails at a small task but cleverly boasts of a big one.

te.translate_as: outward pomp and show, hollow inside
te.note: Said when someone pretends to be smart and grand but has nothing real.

te.literal: like a scorpion stinging a thief
te.translate_as: a wrongdoer suffers but cannot complain
te.note: Said when a cunning person gets hurt in a secret misdeed and stays silent.

te.literal: like the thief himself shouting thief thief
te.translate_as: the guilty person accuses others to hide
te.note: Said when the real mischief-maker loudly blames others to look innocent.

te.translate_as: haste clouds judgment; a hasty person loses sense
te.note: Grandmothers say it when a child rushes and makes a silly mistake.

te.translate_as: work done in a hurry goes wrong
te.note: Said when someone rushes homework or chores and has to redo it.

te.translate_as: even easy things need care and deliberation
te.note: Another common form of the same idea, said to hasty children.

te.translate_as: Think carefully before you act.
te.note: Said before big decisions so one does not act in haste.

te.translate_as: Too much haste spoils the work.
te.note: Said when rushing causes accidents or loss.

te.translate_as: The right time / luck must favour for success.
te.note: Said when effort fails, to teach patience till luck turns.

te.roman: atta meeda kopam dutta meeda chupinatlu
te.literal: Like showing anger at the mother-in-law on the water pot
te.translate_as: Taking out anger on someone else when you cannot confront the real person.
te.note: Said when a kodalu cannot answer her atta, so she bangs vessels or scolds others.

te.literal: Like the son-in-law giving away the mother-in-law's money in charity
te.translate_as: Being very generous with someone else's money or things.
te.note: Used in family talk when in-laws are generous at others' expense, especially about dowry or gifts.

te.literal: Like scolding the daughter while looking at the daughter-in-law
te.translate_as: Scolding one person indirectly to warn another.
te.note: Grandmothers say it about atta who scolds her own daughter so the new kodalu gets the message without direct fight.

te.literal: Performing a marriage is a hundred-year crop
te.translate_as: A marriage decision affects generations, so choose carefully.
te.note: Elders say it at matchmaking time to stress careful enquiry about family and horoscope.

te.literal: He who gives the bride is a butcher, he who takes the bride is lord Shiva in Kailasa
te.translate_as: The bride's family is humbled, the groom's family acts superior during alliance talks.
te.note: Said bitterly about how pillanichina-vallu must plead while groom's side shows pride.

te.literal: Husband-wife quarrel lasts only till the bed
te.translate_as: Couples fight and patch up quickly, outsiders should not interfere.
te.note: Grandparents say it to stop others from taking sides in a couple's small fight.

te.literal: A beautiful wife is everyone's wife
te.translate_as: A beautiful wife attracts others' attention, bringing jealousy and trouble; marrying only for beauty is risky.
te.note: Old people say it to advise to value character over looks in a match.

te.literal: The housewife herself is the light of the house
te.translate_as: A good wife makes the home happy and bright.
te.note: Said to praise the kodalu or wife who manages the kapuram well.

te.literal: Like going to an uninvited wedding
te.translate_as: To go where one is not invited; to interfere uninvited
te.note: Said when relatives poke into marriage talks or visit in-laws without being called.

forms: చెట్టును చూసి విత్తును, తల్లిని చూసి పిల్లను
te.roman: chettunu chusi vittunu, tallini chusi pillanu
te.literal: Look at the tree for the seed, look at the mother for the daughter
te.translate_as: Judge the seed by the tree and the daughter/bride by her mother; mother's character indicates daughter's character
te.note: Classic matchmaking advice from grandmothers when seeing a pelli-choopulu alliance.

te.literal: Like crying as if crying and spoiling the opposite house's wedding
te.translate_as: To pretend sympathy/grief while actually spoiling another's auspicious work or marriage
te.note: Said when jealous neighbours or relatives spread gossip to stop a good match.

forms: తినడానికి తిండి లేదు గానీ తగవుకు పెళ్లాం కావాలట
te.roman: tinadaniki tindi ledu gaani tagavuku pellaam kaavaalata
te.literal: He has no food to eat, but he wants a wife to quarrel with
te.translate_as: To desire a wife/quarrel despite having no means to feed oneself; desiring things beyond one's means/status
te.note: Elders tease a jobless boy eager for marriage, to stress responsibility first.

te.literal: what will not bend as a sapling, will it bend as a tree?
te.translate_as: Discipline/habit must be taught in childhood; what does not bend as a sapling will not bend as a tree
te.note: Grandmothers say it when insisting small children must be corrected early.

te.literal: sense of five years lasts till fifty years
te.translate_as: Character formed at age five lasts till age fifty; childhood nature persists for life
te.note: Said to remind parents that early habits shape adult nature.

te.literal: even to a crow, its child is gold
te.translate_as: Even to a crow its own chick is gold; every parent thinks their own child is precious
te.note: Said fondly when parents praise their ordinary mischief.

te.literal: look at the mother, then look at the child
te.translate_as: Judge a daughter/bride by looking at her mother; mother's character indicates daughter's character, not generally about children learning manners
te.note: Said when judging upbringing or choosing alliances by family.

te.literal: a son who surpasses the father
te.translate_as: Pride when a son surpasses his father in achievement
te.note: Grandparents say it as a blessing for children to rise higher.

te.literal: need to rip open stomach and show to birth mother?
te.translate_as: Need one show one's innards to the mother who bore one? A mother already knows her child's pain without being told
te.note: Said when a child tries to hide hunger or feelings from mother.

forms: చెడ్డ కొడుకు ఉంటాడేమో గానీ చెడ్డ తల్లి ఉండదు
te.roman: chedda koduku untaademo gaanee chedda talli undadu
te.literal: there may be a bad son but there is no bad mother
te.translate_as: There may be a bad son, but there is no bad mother; mothers are never truly bad to children
te.note: Said to stop children from blaming or disrespecting mother.

te.literal: like drinking milk and punching the breast
te.translate_as: To betray/harm one's benefactor; ungrateful behaviour in general, not specifically toward parents
te.note: Said when a grown child hurts the parents who raised him.

te.literal: one without learning is a strange animal
te.translate_as: One without education is a strange animal; education makes a human human
te.note: Grandparents repeat it to push grandchildren to study.

te.literal: learning without a teacher is blind learning
te.translate_as: Learning without a teacher is blind learning; children need a teacher's guidance
te.note: Said when stressing respect for teachers and elders.

te.literal: elder's word is a packed lunch bundle
te.translate_as: Elders' words are like a bundle of cold rice for a journey; nourishing, protective and useful later
te.note: Said to make children listen to grandparents' counsel.

te.literal: if excess happens, sense is lost
te.translate_as: Excess of anything makes one lose judgment/sense in general, not specifically about pampering children
te.note: Said when warning parents against over-pampering kids.

te.literal: a daughter is wealth of another house
te.translate_as: A daughter is wealth belonging to another's house; she will marry and go to her in-laws
te.note: Older people say it while talking about raising and marrying daughters.

te.roman: maatru devo bhava pitru devo bhava
te.literal: mother be god, father be god
te.translate_as: Treat mother as god and father as god; Vedic injunction to revere parents
te.note: Grandmothers teach it to small children as first moral lesson.

forms: దూరపు బంధువు కంటే దగ్గరి పొరుగు మేలు
te.roman: doorapu bandhuvu kante daggari porugu melu
te.literal: A near neighbor is better than a distant relative
te.translate_as: Helpful neighbors matter more than far relatives
te.note: Said when neighbors help like family and friends.

te.literal: If we stay together, there is happiness
te.translate_as: Unity and living together bring happiness
te.note: Elders say it to stop fights and keep friends united.

te.translate_as: Unity itself is great strength
te.note: Often quoted to show friendship gives strength.

te.literal: Like pouring milk for a snake
te.translate_as: Helping a bad or wicked person harms you
te.note: Said when kindness to a wrong person is repaid with harm.

te.literal: Like digging a hole in the house that fed you
te.translate_as: Betraying a helper or benefactor is shameful
te.note: Said about betrayal and ungrateful friends.

te.literal: Like counting the rafters of the house where you ate
te.translate_as: Do not find fault with those who helped you; ungrateful fault-finding
te.note: Said when someone criticizes a kind host or friend.

te.literal: Even God cannot catch a thief from inside the house
te.translate_as: An insider thief/traitor/enemy is most dangerous
te.note: Said when betrayal comes from a close or trusted person.

te.literal: Even a baby snake does not give up poison
te.translate_as: Never underestimate a small or young enemy
te.note: Elders warn not to take any enemy lightly.

te.literal: Like a cat on the wall
te.translate_as: A fickle, indecisive person who sides with both sides
te.note: Said about people who do not stay loyal to friends.

te.literal: As the company, so the mind
te.translate_as: Your company shapes your character
te.note: Grandparents say it to warn to choose good friends.

te.translate_as: Outwardly shiny but inwardly rotten; deceptive appearances in general, not only false friends
te.note: Said to be careful of sweet-talking fake friends.

te.literal: We cannot clap with one hand
te.translate_as: A quarrel cannot happen with one side alone; both sides are responsible
te.note: Said to show any fight or friendship needs both people.

te.literal: too much greed is ruin's cause
te.translate_as: Excessive greed leads to ruin
te.note: Grandmothers say it to warn a child not to grab for more.

te.literal: bad greed is cause of sorrow
te.translate_as: Selfish craving brings suffering
te.note: Said as a moral when someone envies another's things.

te.literal: for desire there is no end
te.translate_as: Human greed/desire never ends
te.note: Said with a sigh when people keep wanting more.

te.literal: stomach will fill but eye will not fill
te.translate_as: Stomach gets filled but the eye is never satisfied; greed is insatiable
te.note: Said when someone keeps eyeing others' food or goods.

te.literal: big greed is a big demon
te.translate_as: Excessive greed is like a big demon possessing you
te.note: Said to frighten children away from greedy behavior.

te.literal: a miser will not open his fist
te.translate_as: a greedy miser never gives
te.note: Said when someone refuses to share even a little.

te.translate_as: what a miser hoards others will enjoy
te.note: Said to teach that hoarding money is useless.

te.literal: like leaving what is there and crying for what is not
te.translate_as: leaving what one has and crying for what one does not have; greed makes you lose what you have
te.note: Said when a child drops one thing to chase another.

te.literal: like a man who cannot afford a loincloth wanting a gold chain
te.translate_as: wanting luxuries beyond one's means
te.note: Said teasingly when children demand costly things.

forms: తినడానికి తిండి లేదు కానీ తాంబూలానికి పొగాకు కావాలన్నట్లు
te.roman: tinadaaniki tindi ledu kaani taamboolaaniki pogaaku kaavaalannatlu
te.literal: no food to eat but wants tobacco for paan
te.translate_as: wanting luxury without basic necessity
te.note: Said when poor demands show off items.

te.literal: as much tree so much wind
te.translate_as: the bigger the tree, the more wind it faces; a big position brings big troubles
te.note: Said to teach contentment and living within limits.

te.literal: without asking even mother will not serve
te.translate_as: you get nothing unless you ask
te.note: Said to explain begging, also to warn against always asking.

te.literal: money is the root of this world
te.translate_as: money is the root of this world
te.note: Elders quote it when talking about money quarrels.

te.translate_as: good health is the greatest blessing
te.note: Grandparents say it to remind children to eat well, sleep well and take care of health before anything else.

te.literal: hunger does not know taste, sleep does not know comfort
te.translate_as: when truly hungry or sleepy, anything will do
te.note: Said when a child complains about food taste or bed, to explain hunger and sleep fix everything.

te.literal: if there is food, there will be muscle
te.translate_as: if you eat enough, strength and health will come
te.note: Said while feeding children to encourage eating properly for strength and growth.

forms: కాలు జారితే తీసుకోవచ్చు, నోరు జారితే తీసుకోలేము
te.roman: kalu jarite tisukovachchu, noru jarite tisukolem
te.literal: if foot slips you can take back, if mouth slips you cannot
te.translate_as: careless words cannot be taken back
te.note: Elders say it to teach control over speech, because mouth is part of good conduct and health of relations.

te.literal: if mouth is good, village is good
te.translate_as: if you speak well, everyone treats you well
te.note: Said to teach polite speaking and respect for others.

te.translate_as: people can say anything without control
te.note: Said when someone talks carelessly or hurts others to remind them to control the tongue.

te.literal: protect like eyelid protects the eye
te.translate_as: protect someone or something very carefully
te.note: Said about caring for eyes, children or health, like eyelids naturally guard the eyes.

te.literal: like sprinkling chilli powder on a wound
te.translate_as: to add more pain to one already suffering
te.note: Said when scolding or teasing a sick or hurt person makes their pain worse.

te.translate_as: small trouble followed by a big blow
te.note: Said when illness or pain gets worse by another sudden trouble on the same spot.

te.literal: like holding leaves after hands are burnt
te.translate_as: taking precautions after damage is done
te.note: Said when people ignore health advice and seek remedy only after falling sick.

te.literal: if you rip your stomach, it falls on your feet
te.translate_as: harming yourself hurts you only
te.note: Said to stop self-harm habits like skipping food or anger that damage one's own body.

te.roman: nidrapoye vadini lepavachchu, nidra natinche vadini lepalem
te.literal: you can wake a sleeping person, you cannot wake one pretending to sleep
te.translate_as: you cannot help one who refuses to listen
te.note: Said about sleep and stubbornness when advice on health habits is ignored.

te.literal: to show heaven in the palm
te.translate_as: to make false big promises
te.note: Said when fake doctors or sellers promise instant cure for body problems.

te.literal: to put a flower in the ear
te.translate_as: to fool someone
te.note: Said when someone is cheated about health or medicine, using ear as symbol of being fooled.

te.literal: you think one thing, god thinks another thing
te.translate_as: Plans do not always work out; fate decides the result
te.note: Said when plans fail unexpectedly to remind that human will is not final.

te.literal: even if god gives, the priest will not give
te.translate_as: Blessings exist but middlemen block them
te.note: Said when officials or go-betweens stop help that was meant to reach you.

te.literal: to the one who did, as much as he did, O Mahadeva
te.translate_as: Everyone gets the result of their own karma
te.note: Said to accept good or bad results as the fruit of one's own deeds.

te.literal: when destruction time comes, intelligence becomes perverse
te.translate_as: When bad fate nears, people think wrongly
te.note: Grandparents say it when someone sensible suddenly acts foolishly before ruin.

te.literal: dharma protects those who protect dharma
te.translate_as: Right conduct protects you in the end
te.note: Said to encourage honest living and trust in moral order.

te.literal: even if you go to Kashi, carrying the kavadi load did not go away
te.translate_as: Fate and burdens follow you everywhere
te.note: Said when troubles continue even after changing place or pilgrimage.

forms: పుణ్యం కొద్దీ పురుషుడు, దానం కొద్దీ బిడ్డలు
te.roman: punyam koddi purushudu danam koddi biddalu
te.literal: man according to merit, children according to charity
te.translate_as: Fortune in life depends on past good deeds
te.note: Said to explain why families differ in luck and children.

te.literal: one bow to god, one bow to ghost
te.translate_as: Keep both sides pleased to stay safe
te.note: Said when people please good and bad powers alike out of fear.

te.literal: to one who swallows the temple, the lingam is a trifle
te.translate_as: A big thief will not spare small things
te.note: Said about corrupt people who loot temples or big funds.

forms: బ్రహ్మ రాసిన రాతను బ్రహ్మ అయినా చెరపలేడు
te.literal: writing written by Brahma, even Brahma cannot erase
te.translate_as: Destiny written on the forehead cannot be changed
te.note: Said to console when misfortune cannot be avoided despite effort.

te.translate_as: God helps through people
te.note: Said when a stranger unexpectedly comes and helps like god.

te.literal: if luck is there, even sitting in the market it will sell
te.translate_as: Luck brings success without extra effort
te.note: Said when an unlucky effort succeeds only because time favours.

te.literal: committed sin does not go away for nothing
te.translate_as: Wrongdoing will surely bring punishment
te.note: Said when someone suffers for past wrongs to teach moral fear.

te.translate_as: Be careful, others may be listening.
te.note: Said as a warning not to gossip or share secrets loudly.

forms: మాటలు కోటలు దాటుతాయి, కాళ్లు గడప దాటవు
te.roman: maatalu kotalu daatutaayi, kaallu gadapa daatavu
te.literal: words cross forts, feet cannot cross the threshold
te.translate_as: Gossip spreads far and fast.
te.note: Said when village gossip reaches far to warn against loose talk.

forms: జారిన మాట, జారిన బాణం వెనక్కి రావు
te.roman: jaarina maata, jaarina baanam venakki raavu
te.literal: a slipped word and a slipped arrow do not come back
te.translate_as: Once said, words cannot be taken back.
te.note: Elders say it to make children think before speaking in anger.

forms: చెప్పేవాడికి సిగ్గు లేకపోతే వినేవాడికైనా బుద్ధి ఉండాలి
te.literal: if the speaker has no shame, at least the listener should have sense
te.translate_as: Do not believe or follow foolish or bad talk.
te.note: Said when someone gossips or gives bad advice to ignore it wisely.

te.literal: when the elephant walks, dogs bark
te.translate_as: Great people ignore petty criticism.
te.note: Said to advise ignoring jealous gossip and continuing good work.

te.literal: we cannot close the village's mouth
te.translate_as: You cannot stop people from talking.
te.note: Said when someone is hurt by gossip to advise not to worry about it.

te.literal: there is no medicine for a slandering tongue
te.translate_as: Habitual backbiters cannot be corrected.
te.note: Said about people who always carry tales and create quarrels.

te.literal: looseness of mouth is not good
te.translate_as: Talking too much and rudely brings trouble.
te.note: Elders scold talkative or rude children with this saying.

te.literal: will gold sound like bronze sounds
te.translate_as: Wise people speak little, fools talk loudly.
te.note: Quoted from Sumathi Satakam to praise quiet, weighty speech.

te.translate_as: A rich person gets many relatives
te.note: Said when people crowd around someone only after they become rich.

te.translate_as: A poor man can only show anger on his lips
te.note: Said when a poor person cannot act against injustice and just grumbles.

te.translate_as: Trouble comes when a poor man tries something big
te.note: Said when bad luck spoils a poor family's important event.

te.translate_as: Everyone takes liberties with a poor man's wife
te.note: Said when poor people get no respect or protection from others.

te.translate_as: Living extravagantly on borrowed money, living beyond means on debt
te.note: Said to warn against showing off richness with loans.

te.translate_as: A hungry person eats anything, hunger does not know taste
te.note: Grandparents say it when a poor hungry child eats plain food happily.

te.translate_as: The rich man becomes the village leader, wealth gives status and authority
te.note: Said when money, not age or wisdom, gives respect in the village.

te.translate_as: Even a mother refuses when asked in need, even close people refuse to lend in time of need
te.note: Said when a poor person feels hurt after asking for money help.

te.literal: do not count the rafters of the house where you ate
te.translate_as: Do not betray or criticize those who fed and helped you
te.note: Said when someone speaks badly about a helper, to remind gratitude.

te.literal: like spitting in the plate you ate from
te.translate_as: To insult the helper after taking help, gross ingratitude
te.note: Very common scolding for betrayal of hospitality and help.

te.literal: even a mother will not serve without being asked
te.translate_as: Even a mother will not serve food unless asked, you must ask for what you need
te.note: Grandmothers say it to encourage children to ask for help clearly.

te.literal: like sitting in tree shade and cutting its branches
te.translate_as: To harm your protector while taking his help.
te.note: Said to warn against ungrateful and foolish acts.

te.literal: even if god grants a boon the priest will not let it
te.translate_as: Even if god grants a boon, the priest will not let it reach you; intermediaries block benefits.
te.note: Said jokingly when help is stopped by someone in between.

te.literal: if you sit and eat, even mountains will melt away
te.translate_as: Living off savings without working will exhaust even great wealth.
te.note: Grandmothers say it to scold idle spending and wasting time without work.

te.roman: pani leni mangali pilli tala gorigadata
te.literal: the jobless barber shaved a cat's head, they say
te.translate_as: An idle person does useless or mischievous work.
te.note: Said when someone with nothing to do meddles in pointless things.

te.literal: a deer will not enter the mouth of a sleeping lion
te.translate_as: Without effort, even the strong get nothing.
te.note: Elders quote it to push children to get up and try instead of being lazy.

te.literal: effort is the mark of a person
te.translate_as: Diligent effort/work is the true character of a person.
te.note: Grandparents say it to teach that working itself is honourable, laziness is shameful.

te.literal: delay turns even nectar into poison
te.translate_as: Delay ruins even good things; even nectar becomes poison if delayed.
te.note: Said when someone keeps postponing work out of laziness.

te.literal: hunger will not go by just crying oh food, oh Rama
te.translate_as: Mere chanting/talk without action will not satisfy hunger; solves nothing.
te.note: Said when someone only complains instead of getting up and working.

te.literal: what did not bend as a sapling, will it bend as a tree
te.translate_as: What does not bend as a sapling will not bend as a tree; habits formed young are hard to change later.
te.note: Grandparents say it to insist children learn discipline early.

te.literal: hero for eating, coward for work
te.translate_as: Brave in eating but coward in work; eager to enjoy but afraid of work.
te.note: Said teasingly to scold a lazy person who comes only for food.

te.translate_as: True learning makes a person humble.
te.note: Grandparents quote it when a child gets proud of marks to remind that knowledge should bring politeness.

forms: విద్య నిగూఢ గుప్తధనంబు రూపంబు జనులకు నతిశయోన్నతి నిచ్చున్
te.literal: education is a hidden secret wealth
te.translate_as: Knowledge is a hidden treasure no one can steal.
te.note: Said to encourage studying because unlike money, learning stays with you and raises you in life.

forms: స్వదేశే పూజ్యతే రాజా విద్వాన్ సర్వత్ర పూజ్యతే
te.roman: swadeshe pujyate raaja vidvaan sarvatra pujyate
te.literal: king worshipped in own country, scholar everywhere
te.translate_as: A king is honoured only at home, a learned person everywhere.
te.note: Grandparents say it to show that education gives respect in any place in the world.

te.literal: one without learning is equal to animal
te.translate_as: Without education a person lives like an animal.
te.note: Said strictly to stress why children must go to school and learn to think like humans.

forms: వినదగు నెవ్వరు చెప్పిన వినినంతనె వేగపడక వివరింపదగు
te.literal: whoever says, what is fit to hear, do not hasten, must inquire
te.translate_as: Listen to everyone, but think and verify before accepting.
te.note: A famous Vemana line grandparents quote to teach children not to believe everything at once.

te.literal: practice is a lowly / humble learning
te.translate_as: By constant practice anything can be mastered; practice makes perfect.
te.note: Said when a child says I cannot do it, to show daily practice can teach anything.

te.translate_as: Education gives vision to understand the world.
te.note: Said to show that reading opens eyes that ordinary eyes cannot see.

te.literal: holding book in hand, low man talks, truth not knows
te.translate_as: Just carrying books and talking is not real knowledge.
te.note: A Vemana line elders use to warn against memorizing without understanding meaning.

te.literal: learning-wealth is chief of all wealths
te.translate_as: Of all riches, education is the highest.
te.note: Said when comparing money and studies to tell children studies never get lost or divided.

te.literal: one who does not know letters is equal to blind
te.translate_as: An illiterate person is like a blind person in society.
te.note: Said to stress why learning to read and write Telugu is essential for living independently.

te.literal: there is no god greater than teacher
te.translate_as: Respect your teacher as God.
te.note: Said on school days and festivals to teach children to touch teachers feet and obey them.

te.literal: by means of effort works succeed in world
te.translate_as: With steady practice any work, including studies, will succeed.
te.note: A Vemana line grandparents use when children struggle with homework to keep trying daily.

forms: ఇల్లు కట్టి చూడు, పెళ్లి చేసి చూడు
te.roman: illu katti chudu, pelli chesi chudu
te.literal: Build a house and see, do a marriage and see
te.translate_as: Running a household is hard and expensive; you know only by doing it.
te.note: Grandparents say it when young people think house and wedding are easy.

te.literal: House secret becomes ruin for Lanka
te.translate_as: Revealing family secrets outside ruins the family.
te.note: Elders say it to warn not to tell household matters to outsiders.

te.literal: Even God cannot catch a thief from inside the house
te.translate_as: If a family member or insider steals or betrays, no one can stop it.
te.note: Said when trouble comes from someone inside the household.

forms: ఇంట్లో ఈగల మోత, బయట పల్లకీల మోత
te.roman: intlo eegala mota, bayata pallakeela mota
te.literal: Inside house sound of flies, outside sound of palanquins
te.translate_as: Poor at home but showing off rich outside.
te.note: Said about families who pretend to be rich outside while struggling at home.

te.translate_as: Other people's home and food always looks better.
te.note: Said when children or family envy the neighbour's house or cooking.

te.literal: She who cannot jump to the hanging pot, will she jump to heaven
te.translate_as: If you cannot manage small household work, how will you do big things.
te.note: Grandparents say it when someone dreams big without doing basic house work.

te.literal: Like pulling down the house to put up a pandal
te.translate_as: Destroying the home itself for a small temporary need.
te.note: Said when someone makes a foolish household decision for show.

forms: పిల్లలు లేని ఇల్లు గుడి లేని ఊరు
te.roman: pillalu leni illu gudi leni ooru
te.literal: House without children is like village without temple
te.translate_as: Children bring life and joy to a home.
te.note: Old people say it lovingly about the happiness children bring home.

te.literal: House without a woman is equal to a forest
te.translate_as: Without a woman to care for it, a house feels empty and wild.
te.note: Said to honour the mother's or wife's role in keeping the home.

te.literal: In Rohini heat, stone mortars crack
te.translate_as: Rohini season has scorching summer heat.
te.note: Grandparents say it in May-June to describe peak summer heat before rains.

forms: మృగశిర పడితే ముసలెద్దు కూడా రంకె వేస్తుంది
te.roman: Mrigasira padite musaleddu kuda ranke vestundi
te.literal: If Mrigasira rains, even the old ox bellows
te.translate_as: First rains bring joy and energy to all.
te.note: Said at the onset of monsoon in June when farmers start ploughing.

te.literal: If ploughed in Arudra, the season will not fail
te.translate_as: Ploughing at the right rainy time ensures crop.
te.note: Farm elders say it to stress timely sowing in June-July rains.

te.literal: If ploughed in Punarvasu, insects will not catch
te.translate_as: Timely tilling prevents pests.
te.note: Said during early monsoon field work about healthy crops.

te.translate_as: Good moderate rain in Pushyami season.
te.note: Said in July to predict useful rain for paddy.

te.literal: Ashlesha rain is half a measure
te.translate_as: Light rain in Ashlesha period.
te.note: Old farmers say it to describe less rain in late July.

te.literal: Makha rain is a full measure
te.translate_as: Heavy useful rain in Makha.
te.note: Said in August as a hopeful sign for filling tanks and crops.

te.translate_as: Abundant rain in Pubba season.
te.note: Said in September about heavy rains needed for growing crops.

te.literal: Uttara only thunders and goes away
te.translate_as: Lots of thunder but little rain.
te.note: Said in September-October when clouds roar but do not rain.

te.literal: If Hasta rains, everything is settled and fine
te.translate_as: Hasta rain settles the crop and the season.
te.note: Said in October to mean late rains confirm a good harvest.

te.literal: Chitta does not care for new sprout
te.translate_as: Sprouts that come up in Chittakarthe do not survive/thrive
te.note: Said in October-November about unseasonal rain harming sprouts.

te.literal: Swati rain becomes a pearl in the oyster shell
te.translate_as: Swati nakshatra rainwater falling in an oyster shell becomes a pearl
te.note: Grandmothers say it to teach that right timing makes small things precious.

te.literal: The thundering cloud does not rain
te.translate_as: Those who boast loudly do little
te.note: Said when someone talks big, comparing to loud clouds with no rain.

te.literal: vows in trouble, forgetfulness in prosperity
te.translate_as: People pray in trouble and forget god when happy
te.note: Grandmothers say it when someone only remembers god in a crisis.

te.literal: when ruin-time comes, mind becomes perverse
te.translate_as: Near downfall people think wrongly
te.note: Elders say it when someone in trouble makes foolish choices.

te.literal: why step in mud, why wash feet
te.translate_as: Avoid trouble in the first place
te.note: Elders advise staying away from risky fights and bad habits.

te.literal: if you pull the creeper, the whole bush shakes
te.translate_as: Pulling one link reveals the whole interconnected network of matters
te.note: Said when a small enquiry reveals a big family problem.

te.literal: without fire smoke does not come
te.translate_as: No rumour without some cause
te.note: Said when bad news spreads and elders suspect some truth.

te.literal: excess greed is root of disaster
te.translate_as: Too much greed causes ruin
te.note: Said to warn against greedy schemes that end in loss.

te.translate_as: Outward splendour hides inner suffering
te.note: Said about families who look rich but suffer debts.

te.literal: even a ghost comes down with a beating
te.translate_as: Strict punishment makes even the stubborn yield
te.note: Said when punishment or hardship finally corrects someone.

forms: చెప్పేవి శ్రీరంగ నీతులు దూరేవి దొమ్మరి గుడిసెలు
te.literal: preaches Sriranga morals, sneaks into acrobat huts
te.translate_as: Preaches virtue but secretly does shameful things
te.note: Grandparents say it about people who moralize in public but misbehave in private.

te.translate_as: Overacting goodness hides bad intent
te.note: Said when someone is suspiciously over-polite or over-religious to fool others.

forms: మాటలు కోటలు దాటుతాయి కాళ్ళు గడప దాటవు
te.roman: matalu kotalu datutayi kallu gadapa datavu
te.literal: words cross forts, legs do not cross threshold
te.translate_as: Big talk, no action
te.note: Used for people who preach and promise a lot but do nothing themselves.

forms: మింగ మెతుకు లేదు మీసాలకు సంపెంగ నూనె
te.roman: minga metuku ledu misalaku sampenga nune
te.literal: no morsel to swallow, champak oil for mustache
te.translate_as: Pretentious show without means
te.note: Said to mock people who show off status while hiding poverty or failure.

te.literal: like the thief himself shouting thief thief
te.translate_as: Guilty person blames others to look innocent
te.note: Used when the wrongdoer loudly accuses others to cover their own fault.

te.literal: they said win at home then win in the street
te.translate_as: First succeed at home, then in the outside world
te.note: Grandparents say it to those who advise the village while their own house is in disorder.

forms: గంగలో మునిగినంత మాత్రాన కాకి హంస కాదు
te.literal: even if bathed in Ganga, crow does not become swan
te.translate_as: Outward ritual cannot hide inner nature
te.note: Said when someone pretends to become pure by outward acts without changing character.

te.literal: what is not in stomach will it be in hug
te.translate_as: Fake affection cannot hide lack of love
te.note: Said when hugs and sweet words are false and the heart has no real care.

te.literal: For one who has dared, even a ladle is god Shiva
te.translate_as: A resolute/desperate person makes do with / wields whatever is at hand
te.note: Grandmothers say it when someone acts with fearless desperation.

te.literal: In courage and daring lives Lakshmi, goddess of fortune
te.translate_as: Fortune resides in courage and daring
te.note: Elders quote it to encourage children to be brave.

te.literal: To one who confronts, the one who fears is easy
te.translate_as: One who confronts boldly overpowers one who merely threatens
te.note: Said to push a scared child to face someone bravely.

te.literal: Like putting your hand in a lion's mouth
te.translate_as: To take a very dangerous, daring risk
te.note: Said when someone does something recklessly brave.

te.literal: For a drowning man, even a blade of grass is support
te.translate_as: A desperate drowning person clutches at any support, however weak
te.note: Said when fear makes people try any hopeless remedy.

te.literal: Like a scorpion stinging a thief
te.translate_as: Suffering in silence because complaining would expose one's own wrongdoing
te.note: Said when a guilty person suffers silently from fear of being caught.

te.literal: In front of its own house, even a dog is a tiger
te.translate_as: Even a coward acts brave in his own safe place; a dog feels like a tiger in front of its own house
te.note: Said to tease false, home-only bravery.

te.literal: Like dogs barking while the elephant walks on
te.translate_as: Great persons proceed undeterred while small/inferior people bark criticism in vain
te.note: Said to tell children not to fear jealous barking.

te.literal: In the dark, a rope looks like a snake
te.translate_as: Ignorance/illusion makes us mistake a harmless thing like a rope for a dangerous thing like a snake
te.note: Grandmothers say it to calm a child scared of the dark.

te.literal: Like the jackal branding itself after seeing the tiger's stripes
te.translate_as: Blind imitation of great/superior people leads to self-harm
te.note: Said when someone rashly copies a brave act beyond their strength.

te.translate_as: Be careful and speak quietly, others may overhear
te.note: Whispered by elders to warn children to be cautious.

te.literal: Elders' words are a bundle of cold rice
te.translate_as: Elders' advice is like a packed lunch that sustains you on the journey; heed it
te.note: Grandparents say it when giving advice to make grandchildren value their experience.

forms: తల్లిని మించిన దైవం లేదు, గాయత్రిని మించిన మంత్రం లేదు
te.roman: tallini minchina daivam ledu, gayatrini minchina mantram ledu
te.literal: There is no god greater than mother, no mantra greater than Gayatri
te.translate_as: There is no god greater than mother, and no mantra greater than Gayatri
te.note: Elders say it to teach respect for mother above all.

te.literal: What does not bend as a sapling, will it bend as a tree?
te.translate_as: What does not bend as a sapling will not bend as a tree; habits/discipline must be taught young
te.note: Grandparents say it about disciplining children early.

forms: తాతలు నెయ్యి తాగారు, మనవలు మూతి వాసన చూశారు
te.roman: taatalu netulu taagaaru, manavalu mootulu vaasana chushaaru
te.literal: Grandfathers drank ghee, grandsons smell their lips
te.translate_as: Grandfathers drank ghee while grandsons only smell their lips; descendants merely boast of ancestors' glory
te.note: Elders say it to remind youth of ancestors' hard times versus today.

te.literal: Big words in a small mouth
te.translate_as: Big talk from a small mouth; speaking beyond one's age/status
te.note: Elders say it when a child talks like a grown-up, half scolding half fond.

te.literal: Like selling fruits using the tree's name
te.translate_as: Selling fruit by naming the tree; living off/exploiting ancestors' or another's famous name/reputation
te.note: Elders say it to criticize those proud only of family name.

te.roman: talli paalu taagi talli rommu guddinatlu
te.literal: Like drinking mother's milk and kicking her breast
te.translate_as: Being ungrateful to one who raised or helped you; biting the hand that feeds you
te.note: Elders say it when children insult parents after growing up.

forms: కన్నతల్లి కడుపు చూస్తుంది, కట్టుకున్న పెళ్లాం మొహం చూస్తుంది
te.roman: kanna talli kadupu chustundi, kattukunna bhaarya moham chustundi
te.literal: Birth mother looks at stomach, married wife looks at face
te.translate_as: Mother worries whether the child has eaten, wife watches the husband's face/mood
te.note: Old people say it about different love across life stages.

te.translate_as: Children have immature, fickle minds; childish behavior is irrational
te.note: Grandparents say it fondly to excuse children's mistakes.

te.literal: Live coolly for a hundred years
te.translate_as: Traditional elder's blessing: May you live a hundred years in well-being and peace
te.note: This is the classic blessing every grandmother gives on touching feet.

te.roman: ooranta oka daaraithe ulipikattedi oka daari
te.literal: if the whole village takes one path, the firewood stick takes another path
te.translate_as: One perverse/stubborn person goes against everyone else
te.note: Said about a difficult neighbour who never agrees with the village.

te.literal: for a wedding in the village, the running around of dogs
te.translate_as: Unrelated, unconcerned outsiders make much fuss over someone else's event
te.note: Said when neighbours meddle too much in someone else's family function.

te.literal: when asked who stole the pumpkins, he felt his shoulders
te.translate_as: A guilty person betrays himself by his own reaction
te.note: Grandparents say it when someone in the neighbourhood exposes his own fault.

te.translate_as: Things far away look smooth/good; distance makes things look attractive
te.note: Said when people praise another village and complain about their own.

te.literal: though he has no cloth to wear, he is the village elder
te.translate_as: Though destitute himself, he poses as a leader/big man to the village
te.note: Said to mock a neighbour who shows off as a big man in the village.

te.literal: what is he to me, the husband praised by the whole village
te.translate_as: What use to me is a husband praised by all if he is no good to me at home
te.note: Old women say it when a man is good to outsiders but not to family.

forms: ఇంట్లో ఈగల మోత బయట పల్లకీల మోత
te.roman: intlo eegala mota bayata pallakila mota
te.literal: inside the house the buzz of flies, outside the sound of palanquins
te.translate_as: Starvation at home but showy pomp outside; poverty at home, show-off outside
te.note: Said about families who pretend to be rich before neighbours.

te.literal: the tree in the backyard is not good for medicine
te.translate_as: People do not value what is near, familiar and easily available
te.note: Said when villagers ignore a local wise person and run to outsiders.

forms: చుట్టం చూపుగా వచ్చి మంచం పట్టుగా కూర్చున్నాడు
te.roman: chuttam choopuga vachchi mancham pattuga koorchunnadu
te.literal: the relative came for a look and sat holding the cot
te.translate_as: One who came for a brief visit settles into a long, burdensome stay
te.note: Said jokingly when guests or neighbours come briefly and stay too long.

te.literal: like going to an uninvited gathering and picking up the child
te.translate_as: To go uninvited and take liberties; to interfere/meddlе without being asked
te.note: Said when a neighbour enters others' matters without invitation.

te.literal: like a donda fruit falling to a crow's beak
te.translate_as: a valuable thing reaching an undeserving person who cannot appreciate it; unexpected good luck to an unworthy person
te.note: Said when someone gets a lucky gain by chance without effort or merit.

te.literal: they say when you bowed to a poor unlucky man, his knee broke
te.translate_as: bad luck follows an unlucky person in everything, even a salutation causes injury
te.note: Said when even a good act turns bad for someone because of ill luck.

te.literal: if it is not fated, even the morsel at the mouth will not stay
te.translate_as: without luck / merit even what is at the mouth is lost
te.note: Grandmothers say it when food or gain slips away at the last moment.

te.literal: who can erase the writing written by Brahma
te.translate_as: fate written by Brahma on the forehead cannot be erased by anyone
te.note: Said to accept good or bad fortune as destiny beyond control.

te.literal: even if a lucky man touches mud it becomes gold
te.translate_as: everything succeeds for a lucky person, even dust touched turns to gold
te.note: Said when a lucky person's ordinary efforts turn into gold.

te.literal: even if an unlucky man touches gold it becomes mud
te.translate_as: everything fails for an unlucky person, even gold touched turns to dust
te.note: Said as the pair to the above when good chances turn worthless.

te.literal: like the priest blocking when god himself grants a boon
te.translate_as: when god himself favours, a middleman / priest blocks it at the last step
te.note: Said when fate is kind but people in between spoil the benefit.

te.literal: like a lump of butter breaking and falling into ghee
te.translate_as: double good luck, good upon good; a lump of butter breaking and falling into ghee
te.note: Said with joy when one fortune falls into an even bigger fortune.

te.literal: like a blind man getting eyes
te.translate_as: a sudden unimaginable good fortune, like a blind man getting eyesight
te.note: Said when someone gets exactly what they longed for against all odds.

te.literal: like a mouse coming in front due to the cat's luck
te.translate_as: gain coming on its own by sheer luck, like a rat coming in front of a cat
te.note: Said teasingly when someone gets profit without searching for it.

forms: అదృష్టం ఉంటే అడవిలో అయినా అన్నం దొరుకుతుంది
te.roman: adrushtam unte adavilo ayinaa annam dorukutundi
te.literal: if you have luck, you will get rice even in the forest
te.translate_as: if luck is there food is found even in the forest
te.note: Said to reassure that a lucky person will survive in any place.

forms: అనుభవించే యోగం ఉంటే అడవిలో అయినా అనుభవిస్తాడు
te.roman: anubhavinche yogam unte adavilo ayinaa anubhavistaadu
te.literal: if one has the yoga to enjoy, he will enjoy even in the forest
te.translate_as: if enjoyment is fated, he will enjoy it even in a forest; fated enjoyment reaches you anywhere
te.note: Said to explain why riches stay only with those fated to enjoy them.

te.literal: like trying to make a priest and it became a monkey
te.translate_as: a botched attempt; intending to make a venerable Brahmin but producing a monkey, i.e. a good plan completely spoiled
te.note: Said when hard work meant for good ends in bad luck and mockery.

forms: పరుగెత్తి పాలు తాగేకంటే నిలబడి నీళ్లు తాగడం మేలు
te.roman: parugetti paalu taage kante nilabadi neellu taagadam melu
te.literal: better to stand and drink water than to run and drink milk
te.translate_as: better to drink water standing still than to run and drink milk; be content with small sure lot than chase risky gain
te.note: Said to advise satisfaction with one's own lot instead of greedy running.

te.literal: like taking out anger at mother-in-law on the water pot
te.translate_as: venting anger on an innocent third person instead of the real cause, like showing anger against mother-in-law on the water-pot
te.note: Grandmothers say it when someone scolds children or servants out of anger at someone else.

te.literal: excessive anger is ruin to life
te.translate_as: too much anger is dangerous to life itself; excessive anger harms oneself most
te.note: Said to calm a furious person and warn that anger hurts health and life.

te.literal: in anger not even a little greatness comes
te.translate_as: by anger not even a little greatness / respect is gained; an angry person earns no respect
te.note: From Vemana, quoted by elders to say anger only brings disgrace.

te.literal: haste is ruin to the work
te.translate_as: haste / hurrying spoils the work
te.note: Said to stop someone from deciding or shouting in a fit of anger.

te.literal: anger on the tip of the nose
te.translate_as: getting angry at the slightest thing, being touchy
te.note: Used laughingly for touchy people who flare up instantly.

te.literal: a beaten dog will not refrain from biting
te.translate_as: a beaten / harassed dog will bite back; if you hurt someone they will retaliate
te.note: Said to warn against harassing the weak in anger, they will hit back.

te.literal: without calm there is no happiness
te.translate_as: without peace / calmness there is no happiness
te.note: A closing proverb elders use after a quarrel to bring reconciliation.

te.translate_as: to meddle / interfere in someone else's matter
te.note: Grandmothers say it when someone interferes unnecessarily while cooking or talking.

te.literal: his dals will not boil here
te.translate_as: his tricks / ploys will not work here
te.note: People say it to warn that clever plans will fail in this house.

te.literal: to dig a hole in the house that fed you rice
te.translate_as: to betray / harm someone who helped you
te.note: Elders use it to teach gratitude toward food and the giver.

te.literal: to knock the rice-morsel out of the mouth
te.translate_as: to take away someone's livelihood
te.note: Said when someone's job or earning is spoiled by another.

te.translate_as: to burn with jealousy or anger
te.note: Used in daily talk when someone cannot bear another's success.

te.literal: to talk like a honey-coated knife
te.translate_as: sweet words that hide harmful intent
te.note: Said about flattering people you should not trust fully.

te.literal: to tell it adding salt and chilli
te.translate_as: to exaggerate a story, to add spice to it
te.note: Used when gossip is spiced up like a curry.

te.literal: he will not give even the oil on his hand
te.translate_as: to be very miserly
te.note: Teasing phrase for a stingy person who shares no food or money.

te.literal: to be like a stone coated with jaggery
te.translate_as: to remain unresponsive and unmoved, showing no reaction
te.note: Said when scolding or praise has no effect on a stubborn person.

te.literal: to drink milk and hit the chest that fed
te.translate_as: to act ungrateful to a benefactor
te.note: Grandmothers say it when kindness is returned with rudeness.

te.translate_as: a sheltered mama's boy or girl
te.note: Grandmothers say it teasingly when a child clings to mother and avoids the outside world.

te.translate_as: to disgrace the family
te.note: Elders say it when someone's bad behavior brings shame to the whole family.

te.literal: to put the house secret outside
te.translate_as: to reveal family secrets
te.note: People say it when someone tells outsiders about quarrels or problems that should stay inside the family.

te.translate_as: constant friction between mother-in-law and daughter-in-law
te.note: People say it to describe the classic everyday tension between an aththa and kodalu in a joint family.

te.translate_as: blessing that a mother's children prosper
te.note: Grandmothers bless children with this to mean may your mother be happy seeing you do well.

te.translate_as: fake or partial affection
te.note: People say it when relatives show outward love but treat someone unfairly inside the family.

te.translate_as: a parent's natural love for own child
te.note: People say it to explain why parents forgive their own children's mistakes.

te.translate_as: a child who brings honor to the family line
te.note: Elders praise a good son or daughter this way for upholding family name.

te.literal: to put fire in the family
te.translate_as: to create quarrels among relatives
te.note: People say it when an outsider or relative turns brothers or in-laws against each other.

te.translate_as: to be overwhelmed by debt
te.note: People say it when someone has borrowed so much they cannot repay.

te.literal: to not have even a pierced coin in hand
te.translate_as: to have no money at all
te.note: Grandmothers say it to stress that the pocket is completely empty.

te.literal: to borrow money and eat pappu-rice meal
te.translate_as: to live lavishly on borrowed money
te.note: Said to criticize showing off or overspending despite debt.

te.literal: to have no bone in the hand
te.translate_as: to give money generously without hesitation
te.note: Said appreciatively about a big-hearted giver or donor.

te.literal: to not let go of the oil in the hand
te.translate_as: to be a miser who never spends
te.note: Used teasingly for someone who avoids paying even small amounts.

te.translate_as: money spent uselessly with no benefit
te.note: Said when an expense gives no result.

te.translate_as: to gain wealth or prosperity
te.note: Said when a family prospers, crediting divine blessing for wealth.

te.literal: to take on debt that goes over the head
te.translate_as: to borrow more than one can ever repay
te.note: Elders use it as a warning against over-borrowing.

te.literal: what does a donkey know of sandalwood smell
te.translate_as: a fool cannot value fine things
te.note: Said jokingly when someone fails to appreciate good food, art, or advice.

te.literal: like a monkey scratching its wound
te.translate_as: making a small problem much worse by meddling with it
te.note: Used when someone keeps bringing up a quarrel and makes it bigger.

te.literal: without the snake dying and without the stick breaking
te.translate_as: to solve a problem cleverly without hurting anyone
te.note: Elders use it to praise a smart, peaceful solution to a fight.

te.literal: like a cat on the wall
te.translate_as: to stay neutral and jump to whichever side wins
te.note: Used in politics or family disputes for people who do not take a side.

te.literal: like rain fallen on a buffalo
te.translate_as: advice or scolding having no effect
te.note: Grandmothers say it when a child listens but does not change at all, because thick buffalo skin does not feel the rain.

te.literal: like the fence grazing the crop
te.translate_as: the protector himself causing harm
te.note: Villagers say it when a guard, officer, or elder who should protect cheats or harms, since a fence should protect the field.

te.literal: when pumpkin thief was mentioned, he felt his shoulders
te.translate_as: a guilty person betrays himself by reacting nervously
te.note: Said with a laugh when someone overreacts and exposes their own mistake, remembering how village thieves carried big pumpkins on shoulders.

te.literal: like a blind bull falling into the crop field
te.translate_as: rushing in blindly and ruining things
te.note: Said when someone enters a situation without thinking and creates damage, picturing an ox trampling the standing crop.

te.literal: like a frog in a well
te.translate_as: person with very narrow outlook and limited knowledge or experience
te.note: Used to tease someone who has not seen the outside world, since the well-frog thinks the well is the whole world.

te.translate_as: quiet trouble or danger spreading unseen
te.note: Said in family talk when a problem grows secretly, like irrigation or spilled water spreading silently under a village mat.

te.literal: to break one's wings into pieces
te.translate_as: to work very hard physically
te.note: Elders say it to praise someone who toils all day for the family.

te.literal: to bend the body and work
te.translate_as: to work hard without pride or laziness
te.note: Grandmothers use it to teach that no work is low if you put effort.

te.translate_as: to work continuously day and night
te.note: People say it about farmers, students, or parents working nonstop.

te.literal: to give up sleep and food and work
te.translate_as: to work with full dedication ignoring rest
te.note: Said when someone works extra hard before exams or harvest or a deadline.

te.translate_as: to earn through hard manual effort
te.note: Used to respect honest, hard-earned money.

te.translate_as: to struggle a lot to finish a work
te.note: Said when a simple work takes a lot of running around and effort.

te.translate_as: to go through great hardship and effort
te.note: Common when people describe how much they struggled to get a job done.

te.translate_as: to be fully buried and busy in work
te.note: Said when someone has so much work they have no time to look up.

te.translate_as: to do hard physical labour
te.note: Used with respect for coolies, farmers, and daily-wage workers.

te.translate_as: to work with stubborn determination till success
te.note: Elders say it to encourage children not to give up halfway.

te.translate_as: to become arrogant after success
te.note: Grandmothers say this when someone stops respecting elders after getting money or a job.

te.literal: foot to not touch the ground
te.translate_as: to be puffed up with pride
te.note: People say this when success makes someone walk proud and ignore others.

te.translate_as: to be blinded by pride
te.note: Used to warn that too much pride spoils good sense.

te.translate_as: to show off manly pride
te.note: Said with a smile when a man boasts about his courage or win.
