te.translate_as: to brag with self-pride
te.note: Used when someone proudly shows off their achievement.

te.translate_as: to swagger with arrogance
te.note: People say this when someone walks and talks like no one is equal to them.

te.translate_as: to behave with haughty arrogance
te.note: Elders use it to scold youngsters who talk back proudly.

te.translate_as: to be stubbornly arrogant
te.note: Said about someone who will not listen or bow down to anyone.

te.translate_as: to look down on others with contempt
te.note: Used when someone insults others as inferior with a proud face.

te.translate_as: to become conceited and rude
te.note: Very common scolding word when pride makes a person rude in talk.

te.translate_as: to have lost one's sense, to act stupidly without thinking
te.note: People say it when someone does a very foolish thing that makes no sense.

te.translate_as: dull-headed person who cannot understand
te.note: Elders scold lovingly when a child cannot grasp a simple thing.

te.literal: he cannot bite even if you put a finger in his mouth
te.translate_as: pretending to be very innocent and harmless while actually not
te.note: People say it about someone who looks too simple to cheat or harm anyone.

te.translate_as: to tell made-up false stories to fool or evade
te.note: People say it when someone tries to fool others with childish lies.

te.translate_as: nothing at all, nonsense, useless thing
te.note: People shout it to dismiss foolish talk that has no meaning or value.

te.literal: to put finger in an anthill
te.translate_as: to foolishly invite big trouble
te.note: Elders warn when someone unnecessarily provokes a dangerous person or problem.

forms: తాటిచెట్టు ఎందుకు ఎక్కావంటే దూడ గడ్డి కోసం అన్నాడట
te.roman: tatichettu enduku ekkavante duda gaddi kosam annadata
te.literal: when asked why he climbed the palm tree, he said for calf fodder
te.translate_as: giving a stupid illogical excuse
te.note: People quote it when someone gives a foolish reason that makes no sense.

te.translate_as: blindly following others like sheep
te.note: People say it when everyone copies one person without thinking.

te.literal: to put a cap on someone
te.translate_as: to cheat or deceive someone
te.note: People say it when someone is tricked into losing money or work.

te.translate_as: to deceive, to pull the wool over eyes
te.note: Used when someone does a trick right in front of others.

te.translate_as: cunning fake humility to trick someone
te.note: Said when a cunning person acts extra humble to get their way.

te.translate_as: to scheme or plot cleverly against someone
te.note: People say it when someone keeps planning cunning moves.

te.translate_as: to make clever calculated moves, to manipulate
te.note: Said like chess when someone shrewdly plans their next step.

te.literal: if delayed, even nectar becomes poison
te.translate_as: even a good thing is ruined if too late
te.note: Said when someone delays food, medicine, or help too long.

forms: రేపటి పని నేడే చేయాలి, నేటి పని ఇప్పుడే చేయాలి
te.roman: repati pani nede cheyaali, neti pani ippude cheyaali
te.literal: tomorrow's work do today, today's work do now
te.translate_as: do not postpone work
te.note: Grandparents teach it to children to avoid laziness.

te.translate_as: to marry, to tie the mangalsutra
te.note: People say it when talking about the groom tying the tali during the wedding ceremony.

te.translate_as: to marry
te.note: People use it in everyday talk to mean a man married a woman.

te.translate_as: to get married
te.note: People say it when someone is about to marry or finally agreed to marry.

te.translate_as: to marry as per Hindu rite
te.note: People mention it when talking about completing the traditional saptapadi ritual in a wedding.

te.translate_as: marriage match to be fixed
te.note: Family elders say it when both sides agree to a marriage proposal.

te.translate_as: to start married household life
te.note: People say it after marriage when the couple starts living together independently.

te.translate_as: to marry and take responsibility
te.note: People say it to mean a man married a girl and promised to look after her.

te.literal: to send to the stepped-in house
te.translate_as: to send the bride to her husband's house
te.note: People say it when talking about bidding farewell to the bride after the wedding.

te.translate_as: married woman visiting her parents' home
te.note: People say it when a wife goes to her mother's place for festivals, delivery, or visits.

te.translate_as: to give one's daughter in marriage
te.note: People say it when talking about the father's ritual of giving the bride to the groom in a wedding.

te.literal: what does not bend as a sapling, will it bend as a tree?
te.translate_as: children must be disciplined young, later is too late
te.note: Elders say it when parents ignore a small child's bad habit.

te.literal: inborn nature will not go except with the funeral bier
te.translate_as: inborn nature never changes, it stays till death
te.note: Said when a child keeps repeating the same mischief despite scolding.

te.translate_as: a much pampered beloved child
te.note: Grandmothers use it fondly for the favourite grandchild.

te.literal: to raise keeping on the head
te.translate_as: to pamper and raise someone with excessive care and affection
te.note: Said when parents spoil a child by never saying no.

te.literal: to look after like eyelid to the eye
te.translate_as: to protect someone very precious with constant care, like the eyelid protects the eye
te.note: Used to describe how parents guard small children.

te.translate_as: it is so obvious even a baby knows it
te.note: Said to tease someone who asks about something every child knows.

te.literal: if you pamper, they climb onto the head
te.translate_as: too much pampering makes children disobedient
te.note: Elders warn young parents not to over-pamper naughty children.

te.translate_as: to stab in the back; to betray someone's trust
te.note: Grandmothers say it when a close friend cheats, because back-stabbing is seen as the worst betrayal.

te.translate_as: to support and stand by someone in trouble
te.note: People say it to praise a true friend who does not leave in hard times.

te.literal: to mix like milk and water
te.translate_as: to mingle inseparably and become very close
te.note: Elders use it when two friends are inseparable and never fight.

te.translate_as: to instigate a quarrel between people
te.note: Said when someone whispers and turns friends into enemies.

te.literal: to dig a pit for others
te.translate_as: to plot harm against others; to dig a pit for others
te.note: Used to warn that one who plots against others will fall in it himself.

te.translate_as: to hold enmity / grudge for long
te.note: People say it when old fights are not forgotten and enmity continues.

te.translate_as: to bear grudge and wait to take revenge
te.note: Said in villages when families or friends turn into rivals.

te.translate_as: to join hands, join forces, cooperate / compromise
te.note: Used when fighting people become friends again.

te.translate_as: to shake off and get rid of someone; to disassociate from someone
te.note: Elders say it sadly when someone leaves a friend in need.

te.translate_as: to greedily crave what others have
te.note: Grandmothers say it when kids or adults stare greedily at someone else's food or things.

te.translate_as: mouth watering, to salivate with craving on seeing or smelling tasty food
te.note: People say it both for food craving and for greedily eyeing money or deals.

te.literal: to put eye on others' wealth
te.translate_as: to covet someone else's property
te.note: Used as a warning that a greedy person is eyeing your money or land.

te.translate_as: endless insatiable greedy wishes
te.note: Said when someone keeps asking for more and is never satisfied.

te.literal: not to shoo away a crow even with a dirty hand
te.translate_as: to be extremely miserly and give nothing
te.note: Classic village taunt for a rich miser who won't spend a paisa for others.

te.translate_as: to suffer intense hunger or starvation, stomach shrunken with hunger
te.note: Said about misers who starve themselves and count every grain to save money.

te.literal: stomach fills but eye does not fill
te.translate_as: greed is never satisfied, stomach may fill but the eye/desire never fills
te.note: Elders say it to explain why greedy people keep wanting more even after getting enough.

te.translate_as: to be ruined, to lose by excessive greed
te.note: People warn atyaashaku pothe anthaa nashtam when greed makes someone risk it all.

te.translate_as: to deprive someone of livelihood, to snatch away someone's means of living
te.note: Said angrily when a greedy person deprives a poor worker of food or pay.

te.translate_as: heart pounding from fear, tension or exertion
te.note: Grandmothers say it when someone is nervous or scared before an exam or doctor visit.

te.translate_as: to break out in cold sweat from fear, pain or weakness
te.note: People say it when fever, fear or low BP makes the body sweat suddenly.

te.translate_as: eyes aching / tired from prolonged waiting or strain
te.note: Said when waiting long for someone or staring at phone till eyes hurt.

te.translate_as: to have a splitting headache, head feeling like splitting
te.note: Used for severe headache from noise, heat or tension.

te.translate_as: to burn with jealousy or envy; also burning sensation in stomach
te.note: Said both for acidity/hunger and for burning jealousy inside.

te.translate_as: body heating up, to run a fever, body feeling hot
te.note: Grandmother touches forehead and says this when you feel feverish.

te.literal: life to come into the throat
te.translate_as: to be terrified or feel life leaving from shock
te.note: Said when a sudden fright or accident makes the heart stop for a moment.

te.literal: speck to fall in the eye
te.translate_as: a tiny irritation causing big pain or trouble
te.note: Used for dust in the eye and for a person who constantly irritates.

te.translate_as: legs going numb or cramping from sitting long
te.note: Said after sitting cross-legged long or walking till legs cramp.

te.translate_as: mouth going dry from thirst, fear or talking too much
te.note: People say it in summer heat or when fear dries the throat before speaking.

te.literal: what is written on the forehead cannot be escaped
te.translate_as: fate is unavoidable
te.note: People say it to accept bad luck or fate, as fate is believed to be written by Brahma on the forehead.

te.translate_as: there is no other help but god
te.note: Everyday talk by elders in helpless situations to mean we must leave it to god.

te.translate_as: everything happens by god's will
te.note: Said to accept surprising good or bad events as beyond human control.

te.translate_as: bad luck struck
te.note: People say it when something goes wrong for no reason, blaming bad fate.

te.translate_as: time has come to pay for wrongdoing
te.note: Said when a bad person finally faces punishment, as sin ripens like fruit.

te.literal: even if god comes down it will not happen
te.translate_as: it is completely impossible
te.note: Said to stress that no power can change a hopeless situation.

te.literal: even a ladle of the sacred cow Gangi's milk is enough
te.translate_as: a little of a noble thing is enough
te.note: Said to value quality over quantity, Gangi is the sacred cow Kamadhenu.

te.literal: O Mahadeva, people get only what they have earned
te.translate_as: you reap what you sow, it is your karma
te.note: Grandmothers say it as a prayer-proverb that fate follows one's own deeds.

te.literal: you get as much merit as building a temple
te.translate_as: a very meritorious good deed
te.note: Said to bless someone who helps others, comparing the help to building a temple.

te.translate_as: to whisper and gossip secretly
te.note: Used when two people whisper together and others suspect gossip.

te.literal: to make a mustard seed into a mountain
te.translate_as: to exaggerate a small matter hugely
te.note: Said when gossip blows a small issue out of proportion.

te.literal: to apply chilli paste and tell
te.translate_as: to add spice and exaggeration to a story
te.note: Used when someone adds masala to gossip to make it interesting.

te.translate_as: to let out something by slip of tongue
te.note: Said when someone accidentally reveals a secret while talking.

te.literal: to put a lock to the mouth
te.translate_as: to stay silent and keep a secret
te.note: Elders say it to tell someone to stop talking and keep quiet.

te.literal: to let the mouth run loose
te.translate_as: to blabber too much without control
te.note: Said to scold someone who talks carelessly and reveals everything.

te.literal: to have no check or control to the mouth
te.translate_as: to speak rudely without restraint
te.note: Used for people who gossip harshly without thinking of others.

te.translate_as: to instigate quarrel with provocative talk
te.note: Said when someone's gossip creates a fight between others.

te.translate_as: to expose hidden secrets publicly
te.note: Used when gossip reveals someone's private matter to everyone.

te.literal: if the wings do not move, the belly will not move
te.translate_as: a daily-wage poor person must work daily to eat
te.note: Elders say it to describe hard life of coolie workers and poor farmers.

te.translate_as: to live very frugally and save
te.note: Said when poor families skip comforts to save money or feed children.

te.literal: for the mealtime not to pass
te.translate_as: unable to make ends meet for food
te.note: Used to describe a family struggling to get even one meal a day.

te.translate_as: to live extremely richly
te.note: Said admiringly or jealously when someone lives in great luxury.

te.translate_as: to live by begging in poverty
te.note: Said to describe utter helplessness or to scold someone for not working.

te.translate_as: extreme destitution
te.note: People use it to stress that a family has nothing at all.

te.literal: poor man's anger is only on the lip
te.translate_as: the poor cannot act on anger, only speak
te.note: Said when a poor person cannot fight back against rich or powerful people.

te.translate_as: to help each other mutually
te.note: Said for neighbours or siblings sharing work and helping together.

te.translate_as: to give help or support
te.note: Commonly used for elders helping youth to stand on their own.

te.translate_as: to rescue or help in trouble
te.note: Said with gratitude when someone helps during illness or money trouble.

te.literal: to be like company and shade
te.translate_as: to stay with and protect someone
te.note: Used to praise a loyal companion who never leaves your side.

te.literal: to stay together in pain and happiness
te.translate_as: to stand by through good and bad times
te.note: Often said about true friends and spouses who help always.

te.literal: do not dig a hole in the house that fed you
te.translate_as: do not harm those who helped you
te.note: Said to warn against ungratefulness and betrayal of a benefactor.

te.literal: do not count the rafters of the house you ate in
te.translate_as: do not find fault with those who helped you
te.note: Used when someone criticizes their helper, it teaches loyalty.

te.translate_as: to repay a monetary debt or loan
te.note: Said when people feel they must repay kindness shown to them.

te.literal: to sit putting leg over leg
te.translate_as: to sit relaxed with one leg over the other, leisurely without doing work
te.note: Grandmothers say it when someone sits relaxed while others are working.

te.translate_as: to sit idle without helping or working
te.note: People say it to scold someone who watches instead of helping.

te.translate_as: to waste time idly doing nothing
te.note: Used for students or office workers sitting jobless.

te.translate_as: to sit idle with no work or customers, as in an empty shop
te.note: Shopkeepers say it when business is dull and they sit free all day.

te.translate_as: to sleep very long and deep and not wake up
te.note: Families tease late sleepers who never wake up in the morning.

te.literal: to eat and lie stretched out
te.translate_as: to only eat and lie down without working
te.note: Elders scold lazy youth who eat and lie on the bed all day.

te.translate_as: to become fat from doing no work, to grow idle and bulky
te.note: Said jokingly when someone gains weight from sitting at home.

te.translate_as: a shirker who avoids work
te.note: Common scolding word for a lazy worker or student.

te.translate_as: to sit yawning, bored and sleepy without interest in work
te.note: Teachers and parents say it for kids yawning in class.

te.translate_as: to pass time, to eke out a living; to spend time
te.note: Elders use it when someone loafs around instead of doing work.

te.translate_as: to memorize by rote without understanding
te.note: Grandmothers and teachers say this when kids cram for exams without understanding.

te.translate_as: to not know even the basics, the alphabet
te.note: Elders say this because Onamalu are the first letters children learn.

te.literal: not knowing a bit of a letter
te.translate_as: to be completely illiterate
te.note: People say this in daily talk to mean someone never went to school.

te.translate_as: to enter the head: to be understood, or to become arrogant
te.note: Teachers say this when a lesson finally makes sense to the student.

te.translate_as: to grasp an idea, to get into the head
te.note: People say this when explaining again and again until the other person gets it.

te.translate_as: to make someone realize the truth, to open their eyes
te.note: People say this when advice or a fact makes someone realize the truth.

te.translate_as: to learn a lesson from a mistake or experience
te.note: Grandmothers say this when a mistake teaches you what books cannot.

te.translate_as: to memorize perfectly by heart
te.note: Teachers use this for poems and tables that children must recite without looking.

te.translate_as: to heed, to pay attention and keep in mind
te.note: Elders say this when they want children to really listen and remember their words.

te.literal: to tear down the house and put up a shamiana
te.translate_as: to ruin one's own home for show-off spending
te.note: Said when someone spends beyond means on functions and parties.

te.literal: a tiger at home, a cat in the street
te.translate_as: bossy at home but timid outside
te.note: Teasingly said about someone who shouts at family but stays quiet outside.

te.translate_as: to visit or enter someone's house
te.note: People say ‘మా గడప తొక్కవా’ to invite or complain someone never visits.

te.literal: a mother-in-law was also a daughter-in-law of some house
te.translate_as: everyone should remember they were once in the same place
te.note: Said to calm fights between mother-in-law and daughter-in-law.

te.translate_as: a son-in-law who lives in his wife's parents' house
te.note: Used in everyday talk about marriage and where the couple stays.

te.literal: for the nest to get scattered
te.translate_as: for a family or home to break apart
te.note: Said sadly when brothers separate or parents pass away.

te.translate_as: to give someone a very tough time
te.note: Grandmother says it when someone is punished or defeated badly.

te.translate_as: a sudden shocking news
te.note: People say it when unexpected bad news stuns everyone.

te.translate_as: to chase something false
te.note: Elders say it to warn against false hopes in summer heat.

te.translate_as: to look sad or gloomy
te.note: Said when someone's face turns dull with worry or sadness.

te.translate_as: words with no value or permanence
te.note: Used when promises disappear quickly like writing in water.

te.translate_as: very short-lived thing
te.note: Said about fame or happiness that bursts very fast.

te.literal: to be blown away by wind
te.translate_as: to go waste, to be lost
te.note: Used when hard work or money is wasted for nothing.

te.literal: to shiver like a hen drenched in rain
te.translate_as: to tremble with cold or fear
te.note: Said in monsoon when someone is fully wet and shivering.

te.literal: like holding an umbrella in moonlight
te.translate_as: a useless precaution
te.note: Elders joke when someone does something unnecessary at the wrong time.

te.translate_as: doubt going away, clarity coming
te.note: Said on winter mornings when confusion clears and truth is seen.

te.translate_as: total ruin or disaster striking a family
te.note: Grandmothers say కొంప మునిగింది when something terrible ruins plans or reputation.

te.translate_as: sudden shocking misfortune
te.note: People say it when sudden bad news leaves someone stunned.

te.translate_as: constant worry or tormenting person
te.note: Used for a never-ending trouble that burns inside daily.

te.translate_as: being trapped with danger on both sides
te.note: Said when any choice leads to trouble and you cannot move.

te.literal: raw wood-apple to fall in throat
te.translate_as: a situation where you can neither swallow nor spit out, i.e. neither accept nor reject
te.note: Elders use it for a problem you cannot swallow or spit out.

te.translate_as: to be helpless with worry or shock
te.note: People say తల పట్టుకున్నాడు when bad news leaves someone sitting in distress.

te.translate_as: to face severe pain, shock or hardship, to feel dazed as if seeing stars
te.note: Used when beating, illness, or shock makes the world spin.

te.translate_as: trouble or blame falling on you
te.note: Said when someone else's problem becomes your burden.

te.translate_as: problem beyond one's capacity to handle
te.note: Elders say it to warn that a worry is too big to carry alone.

te.literal: like a cat drinking milk with eyes closed
te.translate_as: to pretend no one sees your wrong act, self-deception that no one is watching
te.note: Said when someone does wrong openly but acts as if nobody is watching.

te.literal: to do meditation like a crane
te.translate_as: to pretend to be pious and innocent for selfish gain
te.note: Used for someone who acts calm and saintly like a crane waiting to catch fish.

te.literal: a tiger with a cow's face
te.translate_as: a cruel hypocrite in gentle disguise, a tiger with a cow's face
te.note: People use it for a dangerous person who looks soft and harmless outside.

te.literal: one thing in the stomach, another in the mouth
te.translate_as: to say something different from what you feel
te.note: Said when someone speaks sweetly but thinks badly inside.

te.literal: excessive humility is the mark of a rogue
te.translate_as: over-politeness hiding a cunning motive
te.note: Elders say it to warn that too much sweet talk often means a hidden selfish plan.

te.translate_as: to say one thing to one person and opposite to another, to be double-tongued and deceitful
te.note: Used for double-faced people who change their words to suit the listener.

te.translate_as: to get scared suddenly
te.note: Grandmothers say it when someone is startled by sudden bad news.

te.literal: to feel like life has left
te.translate_as: to have a narrow escape from death, to be terrified
te.note: People say it after escaping a dangerous accident or shock.

te.literal: to hold hearts in the palm
te.translate_as: to live in anxious suspense, in constant fear
te.note: Used when waiting anxiously for a result or news.

te.translate_as: to shiver with fear
te.note: Said when hearing a scary story or seeing something frightening.

te.translate_as: to tremble badly with fear or cold
te.note: Common in daily talk to describe someone shaking from fear.

te.translate_as: to be unable to speak due to fear or shock
te.note: Elders use it when someone goes silent from shock or fear.

te.translate_as: to act cowardly and run away, to retreat submissively
te.note: Said mockingly when a boastful person backs out of a fight.

te.translate_as: to flee cowardly from a challenge, to turn back
te.note: Used to shame someone who ran away instead of facing bravely.

te.translate_as: to risk one's life, to act with great daring/courage
te.note: Said with praise when someone risks everything for others.

te.literal: to make the heart into stone
te.translate_as: to harden one's heart like stone, to gather courage and bear pain
te.note: Grandmothers say it when asking someone to be brave in sorrow.

te.translate_as: to grow old, to gain age and experience
te.note: Grandmothers say it fondly about grey hair as a sign of wisdom and long life.

te.translate_as: to become old, hair turning grey
te.note: People say it when noticing age, like you have grown old enough to know this.

te.literal: to stretch legs toward the cremation ground
te.translate_as: to be very old and near death
te.note: Said jokingly or sadly about extreme old age when someone is counting their last days.

te.translate_as: to become bedridden from old age or illness
te.note: Family uses it to say an elder can no longer get up and needs care.

te.translate_as: to pass away, respectful way to say an elder died
te.note: People say it instead of died to speak politely about an elder's death.

te.translate_as: a very aged person, ripe with age
te.note: Said affectionately for a very old grandparent who has seen everything in life.

te.translate_as: an old person walking with a stick as a third leg
te.note: Children hear it when elders joke about needing a stick as a third leg.

te.translate_as: to act as the elder, to guide and settle matters
te.note: People say it when the oldest person is expected to forgive and keep the family together.

te.translate_as: the main protector and support of the family
te.note: Family calls the grandfather or eldest the pedda dikku who everyone turns to for help.

te.translate_as: other people's things look better/tastier
te.note: Grandmothers say it when children envy neighbours' food or life.

te.literal: to beat the drum for the whole village
te.translate_as: to spread private news to everyone, to publicize by beating the drum
te.note: Said when someone gossips about family matters to neighbours.

te.literal: to fall into the village's mouth
te.translate_as: to become the village gossip
te.note: Used when neighbours start talking about someone's mistake.

te.literal: to climb onto the village platform
te.translate_as: a private matter becoming a public scandal/dispute
te.note: Said when a neighbour quarrel goes before the whole village.

te.translate_as: to interfere and call a meeting over a dispute
te.note: Used when neighbours gather elders to settle a fight.

te.translate_as: neighbours/society will mock us
te.note: Mothers say it to stop children from misbehaving outside.

te.literal: if you stay quiet it is good
te.translate_as: staying silent/patient is better, silence avoids quarrel
te.note: Elders advise it to avoid answering back to village gossip.

te.translate_as: to be extremely lucky, everything touched turns to gold/succeeds
te.note: Grandmothers say it when someone gets success after success in job or business.

te.translate_as: to get lucky at the right moment
te.note: People say it when an exam, marriage match or deal works out unexpectedly well.

te.translate_as: to have a good phase where luck favours you
te.note: Very common daily talk to explain why someone is suddenly succeeding these days.

te.translate_as: luck turning from bad to good or good to bad due to planetary period
te.note: Elders use it to explain a sudden change in fortune after hard times.

te.translate_as: fate or destiny written for a person
te.note: Said to accept good or bad luck as already decided, especially to console someone.

te.translate_as: blessing of wealth and good luck
te.note: People say it when someone suddenly gets money, house or prosperity.

te.translate_as: to get a sudden big lucky win
te.note: Young people say it jokingly when someone gets a great job, seat or prize easily.

te.translate_as: to have favourable stars/horoscope, to be naturally lucky
te.note: Elders say a person's raasi is good when whatever they touch or join prospers.

te.translate_as: a cat crossing one's path, a bad omen thought to bring bad luck
te.note: Old belief people still joke about when starting a trip and something goes wrong.

te.translate_as: to look at someone in anger
te.note: People say it when someone glares angrily at children or subordinates.

te.translate_as: to grind/gnash teeth in anger
te.note: Used when someone is furious but holding themselves back from acting.

te.translate_as: to burn with anger
te.note: Grandmothers say it when scolding or insults make one boil inside.

te.translate_as: blood boiling, to become extremely angry
te.note: Said when injustice or insult makes one's blood boil.

te.translate_as: anger going to head, to lose control in anger
te.note: Said when anger makes a person stop thinking clearly.

te.translate_as: to fume with anger, to rant spitefully
te.note: Said when someone angrily shouts and abuses without stopping.

te.translate_as: to burst out in anger
te.note: Common in daily talk when someone suddenly shouts at a mistake.

te.translate_as: to grunt in displeasure or anger
te.note: Used when someone shows silent anger by snorting or glaring.

te.translate_as: Harvest festival in January
te.note: Grandmothers call it the big Telugu festival with pongal, bhogi mantalu, and muggulu.

te.translate_as: Telugu New Year day
te.note: Families eat ugadi pachadi with six tastes and hear the panchanga sravanam for the new year.

te.translate_as: Nine nights plus Vijayadashami festival
te.note: Children start learning and workers worship tools on Vijayadashami for victory of good.

te.translate_as: Festival of lights
te.note: Families light diyas, burst crackers, and share sweets to celebrate light over darkness.

te.translate_as: Birthday of Lord Ganesh
te.note: Families bring clay Vinayaka home, offer undrallu and kudumulu, then do nimajjanam.

te.translate_as: Flower festival of Telangana
te.note: Women stack flowers into bathukamma, sing and dance around it for nine days before Dussehra.

te.translate_as: Offering festival to Goddess Mahankali
te.note: Women carry bonam pots with rice to Ammavari temples in Ashadam month for protection.

te.translate_as: Birth day of Lord Rama
te.note: Temples do Sita-Rama kalyanam and give panakam and vadapappu to beat summer heat.

te.translate_as: All-night fast for Lord Shiva
te.note: Devotees fast, stay awake, and pour milk on Shivlingam at Shiva temples.

te.translate_as: Friday fast for Goddess Lakshmi
te.note: Married women tie toram and pray for family wellbeing on the Friday before full moon in Sravanam.

te.translate_as: Swing festival for girls and women
te.note: Girls fast, swing on uyyala, and eat atlu for a good husband like Karva Chauth in Telugu.

te.translate_as: Full moon day of lights to Shiva
te.note: People light 365 vottulu in temples and eat vana bhojanam under usiri trees in Kartika month.

te.translate_as: first formal meeting of bride and groom families
te.note: Grandmothers say it when arranging the first meeting before fixing a marriage.

te.translate_as: engagement ceremony fixing the wedding
te.note: Families perform it to announce the wedding date and exchange rings or clothes.

te.translate_as: ritual bath before wedding
te.note: Done on wedding morning with turmeric water to purify the bride or groom.

te.translate_as: bride's prayer to Goddess Gauri
te.note: The bride does it for a happy married life before going to the mandapam.

te.translate_as: father giving bride to groom
te.note: Considered the most sacred moment when parents place daughter's hand in groom's.

te.translate_as: pasting cumin-jaggery on heads
te.note: Bride and groom place it on each other's head to mark inseparable union.

te.translate_as: tying of mangalsutra
te.note: The central wedding moment when groom ties the yellow thread with music and blessings.

te.translate_as: showering turmeric rice on each other
te.note: Couples playfully pour pearl-rice over each other for prosperity and fun.

te.translate_as: seven steps together around fire
te.note: Priest guides the couple for seven vows that legally and spiritually complete marriage.

te.translate_as: showing the Arundhati star
te.note: Elders show the couple the ideal-wife star at night as a model for faithfulness.

te.translate_as: tearful farewell of bride
te.note: Said at the end when the bride leaves her parents' home for her in-laws'.

te.translate_as: groom's mock pilgrimage
te.note: The groom pretends to leave for Kashi until the bride's father persuades him to marry.

te.translate_as: Hindu temple, colloquial word
te.note: Grandmothers in Andhra and Telangana say gudi for the local temple you visit, not the formal devalayam.

te.translate_as: home prayer room or corner
te.note: Every call with grandmother starts here, it is where photos of gods, lamps and flowers are kept at home.

te.translate_as: daily prayer ritual to god
te.note: People say puja chesava to ask if you have done your morning prayers.

te.translate_as: lit oil lamp for god
te.note: Lighting the deepam morning and evening is the simplest daily puja grandmothers teach.

te.translate_as: arati with camphor flame to god
te.note: Family gathers to sing and take haarati at the end of puja or on festivals.

te.translate_as: special prayer with names and flowers in temple
te.note: People pay for archana in a temple with their family name and gotram for blessings.

te.translate_as: ritual bathing of god with milk and water
te.note: Done on Mondays for Shiva and special days, people attend early morning to watch.

te.translate_as: blessed food from temple or puja
te.note: You always accept it with both hands and eat a little, it is rude to refuse.

te.translate_as: blessed water given in temple
te.note: The priest pours a spoonful into your palm, you drink it and touch eyes after.

te.translate_as: to bow or prostrate to god and elders
te.note: Grandmothers ask kids on video to put dandam to god when they see gudi or puja.

te.translate_as: tall carved tower over temple entrance
te.note: People fold hands as soon as they see the gopuram from far, before even entering.

te.translate_as: big bell rung in temple
te.note: Children love to ring it on entering, it is said to wake the mind for darshan.

te.translate_as: tamarind rice with tempering
te.note: Grandmothers make it for festivals, weddings, and temple prasadam, and kids learn it as classic Andhra comfort food.

te.translate_as: spicy raw mango pickle with mustard and oil
te.note: Families make it in big jars every summer and serve it with hot rice and ghee.

te.translate_as: sour roselle leaf chutney
te.note: Andhra's most famous chutney, talked about with pride and eaten with rice and ghee.

te.translate_as: crisp moong dal crepe
te.note: A famous breakfast from Andhra, usually served with upma and ginger chutney.

te.translate_as: baby brinjals stuffed with spicy masala
te.note: A signature curry grandmothers cook for guests and festive meals.

te.translate_as: thin tangy dal soup
te.note: Everyday home food eaten with hot rice, especially comforting when sick.

te.translate_as: dum-cooked rice with chicken or mutton
te.note: Hyderabad's world-famous dish that families order and share on Sundays and celebrations.

te.translate_as: fried jaggery dal balls
te.note: Grandmothers fry these sweet balls for Vinayaka Chavithi and other festivals.

te.translate_as: sweet dal flatbread
te.note: A festive sweet roti with dal-jaggery filling served with ghee on Ugadi and weddings.

te.translate_as: deep-fried rice flour jaggery discs
te.note: Crisp traditional sweets made for Sankranti and given to relatives.

te.translate_as: savory urad dal vadas
te.note: Fried like donuts for breakfast or festivals, often paired with coconut chutney.

te.translate_as: crunchy rice flour snacks
te.note: Telangana's famous Sankranti snack that grandmothers make in big batches at home.

te.translate_as: sour-spicy preserved lemon pickle
te.note: Made at home for festivals and travel because it lasts for months.

te.translate_as: spicy raw mango pickle with mustard powder, chili and oil
te.note: A classic Andhra mango pickle mixed with rice and sesame oil.

te.translate_as: thin rice-starch sheets with jaggery and ghee
te.note: Famous sweet from Atreyapuram, grandmother offers it to guests.

te.translate_as: layered syrupy pastry from Kakinada
te.note: Famous sweet visitors always bring back from Kakinada.

te.translate_as: round sweet made of fried chickpea pearls
te.note: Given as prasadam in temples and at weddings.

te.translate_as: crisp fried idli-dosa batter balls
te.note: Evening street snack eaten with ginger chutney.

te.translate_as: crunchy rice-flour rings
te.note: Grandmothers fry them in batches for Diwali and Sankranti.

te.translate_as: traditional draped garment worn by women
te.note: Grandmother wears it daily and talks about choosing new ones for festivals and weddings.

te.translate_as: expensive silk sari for weddings and festivals
te.note: It matters as a precious gift for weddings, often Kanchi or Dharmavaram silk.

te.translate_as: half-sari dress for teenage girls
te.note: People talk about it for the coming-of-age half-sari function before wearing a full sari.

te.translate_as: traditional dhoti worn by men
te.note: Grandfathers wear it at home and for poojas, weddings and festivals.

te.translate_as: sacred necklace tied by groom at wedding
te.note: It is the main sign of a married woman and is never removed casually.

te.translate_as: glass or gold bangles worn on wrists
te.note: Women wear them daily and new sets are bought for festivals and weddings.

te.translate_as: silver rings worn on toes by married women
te.note: They are put on during the wedding and signify married status.

te.translate_as: small nose stud worn by women
te.note: Grandmothers mention it as traditional jewellery gifted to girls.

te.translate_as: kumkum dot worn on forehead
te.note: Women put it on daily after bath and especially before pooja.

te.translate_as: wide gold belt worn over sari at waist
te.note: It is worn by brides and for classical dance and festivals.

te.translate_as: gold necklace made of coin pendants
te.note: It is a family heirloom passed from mother to daughter for weddings.

te.translate_as: ornament tied along a long braid
te.note: Girls wear it with flowers in the braid for weddings and festivals.

te.translate_as: farmer who cultivates land
te.note: Grandmother uses it with great respect, as farming feeds the whole village.

te.translate_as: agricultural field
te.note: Means the family farmland outside the village where crops are grown.

te.translate_as: bullock cart
te.note: Traditional village cart pulled by oxen for carrying crops, hay and people.

te.translate_as: flat ground for drying grain
te.note: Open space in the village where harvested paddy is dried and threshed.

te.translate_as: village meeting platform
te.note: Raised platform under a big tree where elders sit, talk and settle matters.

te.translate_as: village local government
te.note: Village office that looks after water, roads, and local disputes.

te.translate_as: elected village head
te.note: The elected leader of the village everyone goes to for help.

te.translate_as: day before Sankranti
te.note: Villagers light an early-morning bonfire with old things to welcome new harvest.

te.translate_as: festival to start ploughing
te.note: Farmers worship their ploughs and bulls before monsoon sowing begins.

te.translate_as: open water well
te.note: Old stone well for drinking and farm water where villagers gather daily.

te.translate_as: rice-flour rangoli at doorstep
te.note: Women draw it every morning in front of village houses for good luck.

te.translate_as: a limit you must not cross
te.note: Grandmothers say it when warning children not to go too far, from Lakshmana's protective line for Sita in the Ramayana.

te.translate_as: a harsh test to prove innocence
te.note: People say it when someone must prove themselves, from Sita's trial by fire in the Ramayana.

te.translate_as: a tempting trap
te.note: Elders say it about tempting offers that lead to trouble, from Maricha's golden deer form in the Ramayana.

te.translate_as: very deep sleep
te.note: Said teasingly of someone who won't wake up, from Ravana's giant brother Kumbhakarna in the Ramayana.

te.translate_as: a traitor from inside the family
te.note: Said when a family member sides with outsiders, from Vibhishana who left Ravana for Rama.

te.translate_as: ruling in someone's name with respect
te.note: Mentioned as the ideal of duty, from Bharata ruling Ayodhya with Rama's sandals.

te.translate_as: a huge bitter fight
te.note: People say a family quarrel became Kurukshetra, from the great Mahabharata battle.

te.translate_as: an unbreakable promise
te.note: Said when someone takes a firm vow, from Bhishma's lifelong vow of celibacy in the Mahabharata.

te.translate_as: cunning trick
te.note: Said about a scheming uncle or cheating trick, from Shakuni's loaded dice game in the Mahabharata.

te.translate_as: a very generous person
te.note: Elders praise a generous giver as Danakarna, from Karna's charity in the Mahabharata.

te.translate_as: a trap you can enter but not escape
te.note: Said when someone is trapped in a tricky situation, from Abhimanyu trapped in the formation in the Mahabharata.

te.translate_as: total devotion to a teacher
te.note: Said to praise a devoted student, from Ekalavya who gave his thumb as fee to Drona in the Mahabharata.

te.translate_as: 1957 classic mythological fantasy film
te.note: Grandmothers call any trick or magic display Mayabazar because everyone has seen this beloved film.

te.translate_as: 1980 classic film about Carnatic music
te.note: People mention it when talking about classical music, tradition, and timeless Telugu cinema.

te.translate_as: Blockbuster two-part epic film by S.S. Rajamouli
te.note: Made Telugu cinema famous worldwide and people quote it with pride.

te.translate_as: 2022 period action film by S.S. Rajamouli, Oscar winner for Best Original Song
te.note: Young people mention it for Naatu Naatu song and India's Oscar win.

te.translate_as: 2006 Mahesh Babu action hit
te.note: Its dialogues and attitude are still quoted by fans and mimicked in fun.

te.translate_as: Allu Arjun blockbuster film
te.note: Grandkids know it for Allu Arjun's style and viral dialogues.

te.translate_as: Legendary Telugu film star
te.note: Elders call him Megastar with love and grew up dancing to his songs.

te.translate_as: Legendary actor and former chief minister, NTR
te.note: Grandparents revere him as god-like Krishna-Rama roles actor and leader.

te.translate_as: Popular star and politician
te.note: Youth shout Power Star in theatres and quote his fearless dialogues.

forms: ఒక్కసారి కమిట్ అయితే నా మాట నేనే వినను
te.roman: Okkasaari commit ayite naa maata nene vinanu
te.literal: Once I commit, I will not listen even to my own word
te.translate_as: I never go back on my word
te.note: Mahesh Babu's Pokiri line said jokingly when someone is stubborn about a promise.

te.translate_as: I will not back down
te.note: Allu Arjun's Pushpa line everyone shouts for confidence and fun attitude.

te.translate_as: Famous suspense question from Baahubali
te.note: People still say it jokingly for any big suspense or betrayal mystery.

te.translate_as: Famous temple city of Lord Venkateswara
te.note: Grandmother mentions it when talking about pilgrimage and blessings from Balaji.

te.translate_as: Historic monument in Hyderabad
te.note: It is the symbol of Hyderabad that everyone visits for old city shopping.

te.translate_as: Famous old fort in Hyderabad
te.note: People visit it for history, sound and light show, and Kohinoor diamond story.

te.translate_as: Big lake in Hyderabad with Buddha statue
te.note: Families go there for evening walks at Tank Bund and boating.

te.translate_as: Famous Shiva Jyotirlinga temple town
te.note: People go on pilgrimage in Kartika month and for Sivarathri.

te.translate_as: Famous Rama temple on Godavari river
te.note: It is famous for Sitarama Kalyanam on Srirama Navami.

te.translate_as: Ancient Buddhist site and capital of Andhra Pradesh
te.note: Grandmother mentions it for Amaravati stupa and Krishna river history.

te.translate_as: Port city with beaches
te.note: People go there for beach holidays at RK Beach and Kailasagiri.

te.translate_as: Hill station famous for coffee and nature
te.note: Families visit in winter for train journey, coffee, and tribal museum.

te.translate_as: Ancient temple village with hanging pillar
te.note: People visit for Veerabhadra temple art and big Nandi statue.

te.translate_as: World's largest film studio near Hyderabad
te.note: Children love to visit for film sets, rides, and Bahubali set.

te.translate_as: Hills on Godavari famous for boat trip
te.note: People go for Godavari boat ride from Rajahmundry to Bhadrachalam.

te.translate_as: hide and seek game
te.note: Grandmothers name it when children hide around the house and one child finds the others.

te.translate_as: tag-wrestling team game
te.note: Played in school grounds and villages, it matters as the best-known traditional outdoor sport.

te.translate_as: chasing tag team game
te.note: Children play it in school PT periods and during Sankranti village competitions.

te.translate_as: traditional cross-and-circle board game
te.note: Grandmothers teach it indoors with cowrie shells, famous also from the movie Ashta Chamma.

te.translate_as: tiger and goats strategy board game
te.note: Elders draw it on the floor with chalk to teach children planning and counting.

te.translate_as: mancala pit-and-seed game
te.note: Played with tamarind seeds in a wooden board, grandmothers keep it at home for evening play.

te.translate_as: glass marbles game
te.note: Boys play it in street dust by flicking marbles to hit targets in summer holidays.

te.translate_as: spinning top game
te.note: Children spin wooden tops with string in open streets and compete for longest spin.

te.translate_as: hopscotch game
te.note: Girls draw boxes with chalk and hop on one leg, common in school breaks.

te.translate_as: stick and peg hitting game
te.note: Village boys play it in fields by hitting a small peg with a stick, like Telugu gilli-danda.

te.translate_as: children's chasing/tag game where one player is the 'monkey' who catches others
te.note: Children form a circle and tease the monkey in the middle, played for fun at gatherings.

te.translate_as: chess game
te.note: Elders teach it at home to sharpen the mind, it is proudly called an Indian-origin game.

te.translate_as: respectful greeting with folded hands
te.note: Grandmothers say it with folded hands at the start of video calls as a respectful greeting.

te.translate_as: are you doing well, are you fine
te.note: Elders always ask this first to grandchildren to show care about health.

te.translate_as: may you be well, be fine - blessing from elders
te.note: Elders say it after touching feet or namaskaram as a quick blessing.

te.translate_as: live happily and peacefully - elder's blessing to stay cool, happy and blessed
te.note: Grandmothers say it to bless children to live a calm happy life.

te.translate_as: may you live a full hundred years, live a long life
te.note: Elders say it when a child sneezes or on birthdays to wish long life.

te.translate_as: may you have long life
te.note: Elders say it while placing hand on head after padabhiwandanam.

te.translate_as: may you live very long, have a very long life
te.note: Elders say this stronger version for birthdays and festivals.

te.translate_as: stay happy and comfortable
te.note: Grandmothers say it at the end of calls as a parting blessing.

te.translate_as: may god look upon you kindly, may god bless you
te.note: Elders say it to ask god to protect grandchildren far away.

te.translate_as: blessing from elders
te.note: Children are taught to take this by touching elders feet on festivals.

te.translate_as: may you always remain a sumangali - blessing for a married woman for long auspicious married life
te.note: Elders bless newly married girls with this for a long married life.

te.translate_as: may you stay together for a hundred years - wedding blessing to stay together for life
te.note: Elders bless couples at weddings to stay united for a hundred years.

te.translate_as: drawing rice-flour / rangoli design at the doorstep every morning
te.note: Grandmothers do it at dawn to invite Lakshmi into the house and keep evil out.

te.translate_as: string of mango leaves hung over the main door for auspiciousness
te.note: Tied during festivals and auspicious days to invite prosperity and keep negative energy away.

te.translate_as: lemon and green chilies hung at door or shop to ward off evil eye
te.note: Hung on Saturdays or after festivals to absorb evil eye and protect the household.

te.translate_as: ritual to remove evil eye / bad glances, with salt, chilies or harati
te.note: Done for children or new brides when they look tired or dull, to ward off nazar.

te.translate_as: waving lighted camphor lamp before deity or person to bless and protect and ward off evil
te.note: Given when someone returns from a long trip or after a good event to remove evil eye.

te.translate_as: lighting a diya lamp in the puja room / house at dusk
te.note: Lit every evening at sunset to bring light, purity and Lakshmi's blessing to the home.

te.translate_as: housewarming ceremony with milk boiling over
te.note: Done before moving into a new house, boiling milk to overflow as a sign of abundance.

te.translate_as: smearing turmeric and kumkum on the doorstep
te.note: Done on Fridays and festivals because the threshold is seen as Lakshmi's abode.

te.literal: leaving footwear and coming inside house
te.translate_as: custom of removing slippers outside the house
te.note: Followed to keep the home ritually pure, especially near kitchen and puja room.

te.translate_as: sneeze before leaving as bad omen
te.note: Elders ask you to wait a minute if someone sneezes when you start out, to avoid bad luck.

te.translate_as: omens based on lizard falling on body or chirping
te.note: Consulted in homes when a lizard falls on someone or makes sound during important talk.

te.translate_as: crow cawing means guests will come
te.note: Said when a crow caws loudly on the terrace, expecting relatives to visit soon.

te.translate_as: classical dance-drama from Andhra Pradesh
te.note: Grandmothers mention it proudly as Telugu people's gift to Indian classical dance.

te.translate_as: famous Kuchipudi dance-drama about Satyabhama
te.note: It is the best-known Kuchipudi piece, performed in villages on festive nights.

te.translate_as: warrior dance in honour of Lord Shiva
te.note: People talk about it as the vigorous Telangana dance revived after Kakatiya times.

te.translate_as: folk storytelling with music and dance
te.note: Elders recall it as the travelling troupe show that taught puranas and morals in villages.

te.translate_as: musical discourse on gods' stories
te.note: Families attend it in temples, especially during Dhanurmasam and festivals.

te.translate_as: folk ballad praising Mallanna
te.note: It is very popular in Telangana during Mallanna jatara and village fairs.

te.translate_as: group folk dance with sticks and songs
te.note: Girls and women play it in a circle during Sankranti and school functions.

te.translate_as: shadow puppet show of Ramayana Mahabharata
te.note: Grandparents remember watching all-night puppet shows in the village.

te.translate_as: decorated bull dance at doorsteps
te.note: People see it every Sankranti when the bull blesses houses to music.

te.translate_as: flower festival songs and circle dance
te.note: Women in Telangana sing and dance around flowers for nine days before Dussehra.

te.translate_as: tribal group dance of Araku region
te.note: It is famous as the joyful drum dance of tribal women in Andhra.

te.translate_as: devotional song on Lord Venkateswara
te.note: Families sing them at home and in temples to Tirupati Balaji.

te.translate_as: Class 10 state board exams
te.note: Grandmothers treat it as the first make-or-break exam and always ask what marks children got.

te.translate_as: Classes 11 and 12 in AP and Telangana
te.note: People say Inter to mean the two stressful years before college when students choose MPC, BiPC or CEC.

te.translate_as: Engineering and medical entrance test
te.note: Every Telugu family with school kids talks about it as the gateway to engineering or medical seat.

te.translate_as: After-school private coaching
te.note: Parents send children to tuition in the evening for maths and science to get better marks.

te.translate_as: School homework
te.note: Grandmothers on video calls ask if homework is finished before allowing play.

te.translate_as: First writing ceremony for a child
te.note: Families do it at a temple, usually before age five, to start schooling with blessings.

te.translate_as: Prayer to goddess of learning
te.note: Students pray to her before exams and on Vasant Panchami for good studies.

te.translate_as: Long summer school break
te.note: Children spend it at grandparents village, so grandmothers associate it with mango season and play.

te.translate_as: Report card with marks
te.note: Parents show it to relatives and elders to proudly compare marks and rank.

te.translate_as: Standing first in class
te.note: It is the ultimate praise Telugu parents use, asking children to get first rank.

te.translate_as: Small slate for beginners to write
te.note: Older generations started school with it, so grandmothers fondly mention it to grandchildren.

te.translate_as: Teachers Day on September 5
te.note: Schools celebrate with speeches and touching teachers feet to show respect.

te.translate_as: government state road transport bus
te.note: Grandmothers say it for any long-distance public bus travel in Andhra and Telangana.

te.translate_as: ordinary village to town RTC bus service
te.note: Everyone knows it as the cheap bus that connects villages to nearby towns.

te.translate_as: luxury long-distance RTC bus
te.note: People mention it when talking about comfortable overnight travel between big cities.

te.translate_as: three-wheeler shared taxi
te.note: Used daily for short trips to station, school, and market.

te.translate_as: main railway station of Hyderabad
te.note: Telugu families refer to it as the starting point for most train journeys north and south.

te.translate_as: famous overnight train between Hyderabad and Visakhapatnam
te.note: People bring it up as the classic train connecting Telangana and coastal Andhra.

te.translate_as: famous train between Hyderabad and Chennai
te.note: Mentioned when talking about going to Chennai or Tamil Nadu by train.

te.translate_as: famous train between Hyderabad and Kolkata
te.note: Known as the long east-bound train from Hyderabad to Bengal.

te.translate_as: modern fast AC train of India
te.note: People talk about it now as the new fast and clean train experience.

te.translate_as: city metro train in Hyderabad
te.note: Grandchildren hear it when family talks about fast travel inside Hyderabad city.

te.translate_as: last-minute emergency train reservation
te.note: Said when someone has to travel urgently and books one day before.

te.translate_as: pilgrim walk up to Tirupati temple
te.note: Elders proudly mention it when talking about going to Tirupati by steps instead of bus.

te.translate_as: cricket game
te.note: Grandmothers hear it all the time during match season when family watches together on TV.

te.translate_as: Indian Premier League
te.note: People say it every summer when discussing teams like Hyderabad and players on video calls.

te.translate_as: Telugu name for kabaddi
te.note: Elders say చేడుగూడు instead of కబడ్డీ when talking about village school games.

te.translate_as: traditional board dice game
te.note: Family says it during festivals when women and kids sit together to play indoors.

te.translate_as: marbles game
te.note: Elders mention it when teasing boys about playing marbles in the street.

te.translate_as: Olympic badminton star from Telangana
te.note: People say her name with pride as the Telugu girl who won Olympic medals for India.

te.translate_as: badminton champion and coach
te.note: He is mentioned as Sindhu and Saina’s coach who built the Hyderabad badminton academy.

te.translate_as: Hyderabad cricket batsman

en.note: Grandparents say this to warn children to stop while ahead.

en.translate_as: Try something even if luck is needed to win
en.note: Used to encourage someone to take a chance.

en.translate_as: If luck helps, this will happen
en.note: Used before talking about a hope for the future.

en.translate_as: By chance, this happened
en.note: Used when starting a small story about good or bad chance.

forms: wish you the best of luck
en.translate_as: I hope you have good luck
en.note: Common kind goodbye before a test or interview.

en.translate_as: No luck left, chance is gone
en.note: Used when something you wanted is finished or closed.

en.translate_as: A sudden good chance that helps you
en.note: Used for jobs or success that came by chance.

en.translate_as: The third try will bring good luck
en.note: Said to comfort someone after two failures.

en.translate_as: A person who always has good luck
en.note: Used lovingly for a child who gets good things easily.

en.translate_as: Very good luck that comes suddenly
en.note: Common American saying, Irish means people from Ireland.

en.translate_as: in trouble, likely to be punished
en.note: Kids say this when they did something wrong at school or home.

en.translate_as: stuck in a difficult situation
en.note: Friends say this when they need quick help.

en.translate_as: in serious trouble
en.note: Used when the problem is big, like money or school trouble.

en.translate_as: in a situation too hard to handle
en.note: Said when someone took on work that is too difficult.

forms: between a rock and a hard place
caught between a rock and a hard place
en.translate_as: having to choose between two bad options
en.meaning_te: రెండు వైపులా కష్టమే, ఏమి చేయాలో తెలియని పరిస్థితి
en.note: Used when both choices are difficult.

forms: out of the frying pan into the fire
went from the frying pan into the fire
en.translate_as: from a bad situation to a worse one
en.meaning_te: ఒక కష్టం నుండి ఇంకా పెద్ద కష్టంలోకి వెళ్లడం
en.note: Said when trying to fix a problem makes it worse.

en.translate_as: in a risky situation, close to trouble
en.meaning_te: ఎప్పుడైనా కష్టంలో పడే ప్రమాదకర పరిస్థితిలో ఉండడం
en.note: Parents say this as a warning to be careful.

forms: up the creek without a paddle
en.translate_as: in trouble with no help
en.note: Common funny way to say you are stuck with no solution.

en.translate_as: making your trouble worse by your actions
en.note: Used when lying or making excuses makes things worse.

en.translate_as: cause trouble by changing a stable situation
en.note: Adults say don't rock the boat to mean stay calm.

en.translate_as: cause a fight or problem on purpose
en.note: Used for gossip or teasing that leads to a fight.

en.translate_as: act in a way that will bring trouble
en.note: Grandparents and parents say this as a warning.

en.translate_as: just escape a big trouble
en.note: Kids say whew, dodged a bullet when they almost get caught.

en.translate_as: free from trouble or punishment
en.note: Said with relief when teacher or parent forgives you.

en.translate_as: Try as hard as you can
en.note: Grandchild says this before a test or game to mean try hard.

en.translate_as: Do more than what is needed
en.note: Used to praise someone for working very hard.

en.translate_as: Try every possible way
en.note: Used when someone tries very hard to find or fix something.

en.translate_as: Do your share of the work
en.note: Said in school projects or team work.

en.translate_as: Try very hard to help or please
en.note: Used when someone does a lot to help another person.

en.translate_as: Keep trying without stopping
en.note: Grandmother can say this to encourage practice.

en.translate_as: Get ready for hard work
en.note: Said before starting a difficult task.

en.translate_as: Work with full energy
en.note: Said to push someone to work harder.

en.translate_as: Give more than full effort
en.note: Common in US sports and school to mean full effort.

en.translate_as: Do the hardest part of the work
en.note: Used at work or home for the hardest job.

forms: keep your nose to the grindstone
kept his nose to the grindstone
en.translate_as: Work hard without rest
en.note: Teachers say this to mean focus and work hard.

forms: work your fingers to the bone
worked my fingers to the bone
works his fingers to the bone
en.translate_as: Work extremely hard
en.note: Said when someone is tired from too much work.

en.translate_as: Do anything possible to succeed
en.note: Used when someone tries everything to help family.

en.translate_as: Do much better than expected
en.note: Used to praise good work at school or job.

en.translate_as: to finally decide
en.note: Your grandchild says this when someone is taking too long to choose.

forms: weigh up the pros and cons
en.translate_as: to think about the good and bad points
en.note: People say this when choosing school, job, or a big purchase.

en.translate_as: to be undecided between two choices
en.note: Used when the grandchild cannot pick between two things.

en.translate_as: to wait till tomorrow to decide
en.note: Grandparents often give this good advice for big decisions.

en.translate_as: to trust your feeling
en.note: Kids in the US say this when there is no clear right answer.

en.translate_as: to boldly do something after waiting
en.note: Used for marriage, new job, or moving to a new place.

en.translate_as: to bravely do a hard thing
en.note: Said when someone must accept a painful but needed choice.

en.translate_as: to be the one who decides
en.note: Used to ask who is the boss in a situation.

en.translate_as: to make the final decision
en.note: Common on video calls when deciding what to do next.

en.translate_as: to think carefully before deciding
en.note: Elders say this to warn children not to hurry.

en.translate_as: to start doubting your decision
en.note: Your grandchild may say this after choosing a college or course.

en.translate_as: to not change your decision
en.note: Said to support someone when others pressure them to change.

forms: cross that bridge when you come to it
we will cross that bridge when we get there
en.translate_as: to worry about it later when it happens
en.note: Very common to calm worry about the future.

en.translate_as: to decide randomly by coin
en.note: Kids do this for fun for small choices like movie or game.

forms: past the point of no return
en.translate_as: a stage where you cannot go back
en.note: Used for very serious decisions like moving or surgery.

en.translate_as: share gossip or juicy news
en.note: Very common with young people when asking for gossip.

en.translate_as: heard news indirectly as rumor
en.note: Used when you did not hear news directly, only from others.

en.translate_as: gossip badly about someone not present
en.meaning_te: లేని వ్యక్తి గురించి వెనుక చెడుగా మాట్లాడటం
en.note: Used to complain about unfair gossip.

en.translate_as: heard directly from the real person
en.note: Used to say the news is true because the main person said it.

en.translate_as: avoid saying directly, talk in circles
en.note: Used when someone is shy to say the main point.

en.translate_as: honest private talk about feelings
en.note: Used for a serious loving talk between family or close friends.

en.translate_as: polite light chat about simple things
en.meaning_te: మర్యాద కోసం చిన్న చిన్న మాటలు మాట్లాడటం
en.note: Used for short weather or daily-life talk with strangers.

en.translate_as: talk too much without stopping
en.note: Used jokingly when a child talks nonstop to grandma.

en.translate_as: keep it secret, tell no one
en.note: Used to ask someone to keep a secret.

en.translate_as: be quiet and keep a secret
en.note: Used playfully to tell kids to stay quiet.

forms: put your foot in your mouth
put his foot in his mouth
en.translate_as: say something wrong and embarrassing
en.note: Used when someone says the wrong thing by mistake.

en.translate_as: news passed person to person by talking
en.meaning_te: ఒకరి నుండి ఒకరికి మాటల ద్వారా తెలియడం
en.note: Used when many people know news because friends told them.

en.translate_as: A son acts just like his father.
en.note: Grandchild says this when someone copies their parent.

forms: The apple doesn't fall far from the tree
Apple never falls far from the tree
en.translate_as: A child is very similar to the parents.
en.note: Used when a child has same habit or looks as parents.

en.translate_as: Family bond is stronger than others.
en.note: Said when family helps each other first.

forms: The black sheep in the family
en.translate_as: The one person who is different from the family.
en.note: Used jokingly for the naughty or different member.

en.translate_as: A habit or feature passes in the family.
en.note: Said about looks, talent, or illness in the family.

forms: A chip off the old block
en.translate_as: A child is just like the parent.
en.note: Said proudly when son acts like father.

en.translate_as: Looks exactly like that person.
en.note: Grandchild may say you are spitting image of mom.

en.translate_as: A close blood relative.
en.note: Said to show deep love for family member.

forms: Born with a silver spoon in one's mouth
en.translate_as: Born in a rich family.
en.note: Used when talking about a rich child.

en.translate_as: A boy who is very attached to his mother.
en.note: Used teasingly for a son close to mother.

en.translate_as: A girl who is very close to her father.
en.note: Fathers say this lovingly on video calls.

en.translate_as: Keep something only among family.
en.note: Said about secret, business, or property.

en.translate_as: The person who earns for the family.
en.note: Used to say who works and supports home.

en.translate_as: Fight or jealousy between brothers and sisters.
en.note: Used when kids fight or compete at home.

en.translate_as: to start a trip
en.note: People say this when it is time to leave for a trip.

en.translate_as: to travel far by car for fun
en.note: American kids often do this with friends in summer.

en.translate_as: to carry very few bags
en.note: Grandchild may say this when packing only one small bag.

en.translate_as: a place not visited by many people
en.note: Used for a quiet village or hidden place tourists do not know.

en.translate_as: to take a break from busy life
en.note: People say this when they go on vacation to rest.

en.translate_as: a trip with no problems
en.note: Originally about ships, now used for any easy travel.

forms: we are in the same boat
en.translate_as: in the same difficult situation
en.note: Used when all travelers face the same delay.

forms: hit a bump in the road
hit a bump on the road
en.translate_as: a small problem during a plan
en.note: People say this for a cancelled flight or car trouble.

en.translate_as: to stop briefly during a long drive
en.note: Usually to eat, rest, or use the bathroom.

en.translate_as: a place where you feel comfortable like home
en.note: Grandchild may call grandmother's house this.

en.translate_as: to feel tired after a long flight
en.note: Common when flying between India and America.

en.translate_as: to get on a plane on time
en.note: People say I have to catch my flight when hurrying to the airport.

en.translate_as: wish for a safe journey
en.note: A kind goodbye you can say before grandchild travels.

en.translate_as: to want to travel very much
en.note: Used when someone loves travel and cannot stay home.

en.translate_as: healthy again after being sick
en.note: Grandchild says this after recovering from fever or flu.

en.translate_as: to recover from a sickness
en.note: Used to talk about getting better after a cold or cough.

en.translate_as: to become sick with a cold
en.note: Said in winter when someone gets cough and cold.

en.translate_as: very healthy and strong
en.note: Often said by old people to say they are healthy.

forms: give a clean bill of health
got a clean bill of health
en.translate_as: doctor says you are healthy
en.note: Used after a check-up when everything is normal.

en.translate_as: to stop a bad habit
en.note: Used for quitting smoking or junk food for health.

en.translate_as: getting better after sickness
en.note: Said when someone is slowly becoming healthy.

en.translate_as: tired and low energy, getting sick
en.note: Used when work or less sleep makes the body weak.

en.translate_as: not fit, body is weak
en.note: Used about exercise and weight and fitness.

forms: look like the picture of health
en.translate_as: looks very healthy
en.note: A compliment when a child looks healthy and active.

forms: take a turn for the worse
took a turn for the worse
took a turn for the better
en.translate_as: suddenly become more sick or better
en.meaning_te: ఆరోగ్యం అకస్మాత్తుగా खराब కావడం లేదా మెరుగుపడటం
en.note: Used in hospital news about someone's health changing.

en.translate_as: to try not to get sick
en.note: Said when resting and drinking soup to avoid full sickness.

en.translate_as: alive, active and healthy
en.note: A happy, funny way to say I am fine on a video call.

en.translate_as: no lie, for real
en.note: Grandchild says this to show they are telling the truth.

en.translate_as: did very well, looked great
en.note: Used to praise someone for looks or work.

en.translate_as: okay, deal, yes
en.note: Grandchild says this instead of yes or okay.

en.translate_as: feeling or mood of a place
en.note: Used to talk about nice or bad feeling.

en.translate_as: suspicious, not trusted
en.note: Used when something feels strange or dishonest.

en.translate_as: charm to attract someone
en.note: Young people use it for flirting or charm.

en.translate_as: secretly, a little bit
en.note: Used before telling a small true feeling.

en.translate_as: openly, very much
en.note: Used to show strong feeling openly.

en.translate_as: suddenly stop talking to someone
en.note: Used when a friend stops replying to messages.

en.translate_as: fear of missing fun
en.note: Used when sad about missing a party or trip.

en.translate_as: sounds or tastes very good
en.note: Often used for music or food they love.

en.translate_as: average, not special
en.note: Used when something is just okay.

en.translate_as: food is very tasty
en.note: Grandchild says this when they love the food.

en.translate_as: nice clothes and style
en.note: Used to praise cool dressing.

en.translate_as: show off proudly
en.note: Used when someone shows off money or things.

en.translate_as: angry or jealous
en.note: Used when someone is upset about losing.

en.translate_as: best of all time
en.note: Used to praise a player or star.

en.translate_as: embarrassing to watch
en.note: Used for videos that feel awkward.

en.translate_as: sudden dislike feeling
en.note: Used when they suddenly dislike a crush.

en.translate_as: laughing very hard in a text
en.note: Grandchildren type LOL when something is funny, not always real loud laugh.

en.translate_as: showing surprise or shock
en.note: Used when surprised, happy or shocked on chat.

en.translate_as: adding extra small information
en.note: Used to add one more point while texting.

en.translate_as: I do not know the answer
en.note: Children type IDK for quick reply when they do not know.

en.translate_as: speaking honestly and openly
en.note: Used before giving true opinion in messages.

en.translate_as: this is what I think
en.note: Used to share own thought politely online.

en.translate_as: telling you for your knowledge
en.note: Used when sharing news or information on chat.

en.translate_as: I will come back in a minute
en.note: Typed on video call or chat when going away shortly.

en.translate_as: bye, we will talk later
en.note: A quick way to end chat or call.

en.translate_as: leave it, forget what I said
en.note: Used when no need to explain more.

en.translate_as: private message to one person
en.note: On Instagram or apps, DM means chat privately.

en.translate_as: photo you take of yourself
en.note: Grandchild may ask for selfie on video call.

en.translate_as: funny photo or video shared online
en.note: Kids share memes to joke on phone.

en.translate_as: many people see and share quickly
en.note: A video going viral means it became very famous fast.

en.translate_as: teasing or troubling people online
en.note: A troll writes bad comments to make others angry.

en.translate_as: suddenly stop replying to messages
en.note: If friend stops replying with no reason, they ghosted.

en.translate_as: # word used to find topics
en.note: Like #family helps find photos on apps.

en.translate_as: small smiley pictures in text

en.note: Smiley faces like 😊 used to show feeling.

en.translate_as: showing disappointment or no words
en.note: Typed when someone does something silly.

en.note: Grandchild says this proudly after a good exam.

en.translate_as: to fail a test or class
en.note: Used when someone gets very low marks.

en.note: Students do this the night before an exam.

en.translate_as: to stay awake all night to study
en.note: Common in college before big exams.

en.translate_as: to not go to class on purpose
en.note: Teachers do not like this.

en.translate_as: a sudden test without warning
en.note: Students often complain about this.

en.translate_as: average of all school marks
en.note: Important number for college in America.

en.translate_as: main subject chosen in college
en.note: Like science, history, or computer studies.

en.translate_as: building where college students live
en.note: Most US college students live here.

en.translate_as: person who shares your room
en.note: Grandchild will talk about who they live with.

en.translate_as: first-year student in school or college
en.note: Used for new students in big school.

en.translate_as: student who studies a lot
en.note: Sometimes teasing, sometimes friendly.

en.translate_as: student who is good at sports
en.note: Usually for football or basketball players.

en.translate_as: funny student who makes class laugh
en.note: Said about a naughty funny child.

en.translate_as: laziness in the last year of school

en.note: Joke word for final-year students not studying.

en.translate_as: punishment to stay back after school
en.note: Given when a child misbehaves in class.

en.translate_as: big dance party for school students
en.note: Special party for older school children in US.

en.translate_as: school celebration with game and dance
en.meaning_te: స్కూల్ వార్షిక వేడుక, ఆట మరియు డ్యాన్స్
en.note: Old students also come back for this party.

en.translate_as: you did it perfectly

en.translate_as: nothing bad, all perfect
en.note: Added after ate to mean you did everything perfectly.

en.translate_as: very special and memorable
en.note: Said when someone or something is very cool and unforgettable.

en.translate_as: really cool or excellent
en.note: Used for food, clothes, music, or photos that are excellent.

en.translate_as: fun and exciting
en.note: Said when a party, photo, or news is very exciting.

en.translate_as: you are wonderful and strong
en.note: Loving praise often said to a girl or woman.

en.translate_as: that is a win, good job
en.note: W means win, said when someone succeeds or looks good.

en.translate_as: perfect, just right
en.note: Said when clothes, makeup, or food is exactly perfect.

en.translate_as: looking sharp and pretty
en.note: Compliment for looking slim, neat, and beautiful.

en.translate_as: very pretty and confident girl
en.note: Playful compliment that means you look pretty and strong.

en.translate_as: best quality, first class
en.note: Said when something is of the very best quality.

en.translate_as: perfect score, perfect
en.note: Means perfect, like giving full marks.

en.translate_as: good and correct
en.note: Short way to say your look or opinion is good.

en.translate_as: show your talent boldly
en.note: Cheering someone to shine and do great.

en.translate_as: you are doing great
en.note: Praise for doing very well in work or life.

en.translate_as: you did it exactly right
en.note: Said when someone does a job perfectly.

en.translate_as: perfect, lovely
en.note: People kiss fingers to show food or look is perfect.

en.translate_as: That is so funny I can't stop laughing.
en.note: Grandchild says this when laughing hard on video call, not about real death.

en.translate_as: I'm laughing a lot or I feel emotional.

en.translate_as: I'm shocked, excited, or laughing loudly.
en.note: Said when surprised or very excited, not a real scream.

en.translate_as: I can't believe it, really?
en.note: Said with surprise when hearing big news.

en.translate_as: Wow, I am surprised or excited.
en.note: Very common reaction to surprise, good news or bad news.

en.translate_as: Really? Is that true?
en.note: Grandchild asks this to check if you are serious.

en.translate_as: Really? I can't believe it.
en.note: Said when shocked by what someone told.

en.translate_as: That is surprising or unbelievable.
en.note: Said for both good surprises and bad surprises.

en.translate_as: That is shocking or unexpected.
en.note: Used when a story is hard to believe.

en.translate_as: That is amazing or shocking.
en.note: Can mean very good or very shocking.

en.translate_as: Wow, really? Come on.
en.note: Said to a friend when surprised, annoyed, or joking.

en.translate_as: Oh no, that's bad or awkward.
en.meaning_te: అయ్యో, అది ఇబ్బందిగా లేదా బాధగా ఉంది
en.note: Said when something goes wrong or is embarrassing.

en.translate_as: Oh no, that hurts or feels bad.
en.note: Said when someone falls, fails, or hears sad news.

en.translate_as: It looks or feels like this style.
en.meaning_te: ఇది అలా అనిపిస్తోంది, ఆ లుక్ వస్తోంది
en.note: Grandchild uses this to praise looks, like It's giving pretty.

en.translate_as: Yay, I'm excited, we did it.
